questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with fever, headache, and neck stiffness that began 8 hours ago. A lumbar puncture yields cloudy cerebrospinal fluid, and the Gram stain shows gram-negative, kidney bean-shaped organisms arranged in pairs within neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus classically described as kidney bean- or coffee bean-shaped and is frequently seen inside neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria meningitidis stains gram negative and grows in pairs whose flattened adjacent sides give the kidney bean appearance. Because the organism attaches to and enters host cells, it is commonly recovered from within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on cerebrospinal fluid smears. Along with S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae it is one of the three major bacterial causes of meningitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a gram-negative bacillus and does not form diplococci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. influenzae is a gram-negative coccobacillus, intermediate between a coccus and a bacillus, not a paired kidney bean form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod and would not appear as a gram-negative diplococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus, so it would stain purple rather than pink on the smear.

questions.stem: A gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus is isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid of a college student with meningitis. The laboratory performs carbohydrate utilization testing to confirm the identification. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose and lactose fermented; maltose not fermented

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose and maltose fermented; lactose not fermented

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose fermented only; maltose not fermented

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactose and sucrose fermented; maltose not fermented

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sucrose and fructose fermented; glucose not fermented

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose but not lactose, sucrose, or fructose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbohydrate utilization is a standard confirmatory step for Neisseria species. N. meningitidis metabolizes both glucose and maltose, while lactose, sucrose, and fructose are not fermented. Combined with an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus on smear, this pattern identifies the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactose is not fermented by this organism, and maltose is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose fermentation alone is incomplete, because maltose is also fermented.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose and sucrose are both negative, and maltose is positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither sucrose nor fructose is fermented, and glucose is.

questions.stem: A cerebrospinal fluid isolate is being characterized to confirm a diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis. Which of the following sets of laboratory characteristics is expected for this organism?

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is oxidase positive, nonmotile, nonhemolytic, and facultatively anaerobic, with growth optimized in 5% carbon dioxide.
explanation.whyCorrect: A positive oxidase reaction is a defining screening test for Neisseria species. The organism does not move on its own and produces no hemolysis on blood-containing media. It is facultatively anaerobic and grows best in an atmosphere enriched to 5% carbon dioxide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The organism is oxidase positive, nonmotile, and produces no hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The oxidase test is positive and the organism is nonmotile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oxidase test is positive, and no alpha-hemolysis is produced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although oxidase positive, the organism is nonmotile and nonhemolytic.

questions.stem: During an outbreak investigation, nasopharyngeal swabs are collected from asymptomatic students to look for meningococcal carriage. Because the specimens come from a site heavily colonized with normal flora, which of the following media should be used to recover the organism?

explanation.summary: Thayer-Martin agar is the selective medium used when a Neisseria specimen comes from a nonsterile site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thayer-Martin agar is built on a chocolate agar base, with antibiotics, antifungals, and added nutrients that suppress competing flora while supporting Neisseria. That selectivity is what makes it the right choice for a nonsterile specimen such as a nasopharyngeal swab. Specimens from sterile sites, such as cerebrospinal fluid, can simply be plated on chocolate agar.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood agar is differential rather than selective and does not adequately support this fastidious organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MacConkey agar is used for gram-negative enteric organisms and to assess lactose fermentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mannitol salt agar is a high-salt medium used to select for staphylococci, not Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An unsupplemented nutrient broth is neither enriched nor selective and would be overgrown by normal flora.

questions.stem: A microbiology student asks why fastidious organisms such as Neisseria species grow well on chocolate agar. Which of the following best explains this property of the medium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 7.5% sodium chloride concentration enriches for cocci

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotics and antifungals suppress competing organisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile salts and crystal violet select for gram-negative rods

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactose and a pH indicator reveal fermenting colonies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells are heat-lysed, releasing added nutrients

explanation.summary: Chocolate agar is red blood cell agar that has been heated to lyse the cells and release intracellular nutrients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fastidious bacteria require an enriched medium. Heating blood agar ruptures the erythrocytes, spilling their contents into the medium and raising nutrient availability, which also gives the agar its brown chocolate color. Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae grow on it for this reason.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high salt concentration describes mannitol salt agar, which selects for staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Added antimicrobials describe the selective Thayer-Martin formulation, not chocolate agar itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile salts and crystal violet describe MacConkey agar, a selective medium for enteric gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactose with a pH indicator is a differential feature of media such as MacConkey agar.

questions.stem: The endotoxin of N. meningitidis is designated lipooligosaccharide rather than lipopolysaccharide. Compared with the lipopolysaccharide of most other gram-negative bacteria, this molecule differs in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a secreted exotoxin rather than a wall component

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lacks lipid A and therefore triggers no cytokine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lacks the core polysaccharide, leaving only lipid A

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks the O antigen, making a shorter molecule

choices.label: E
choices.text: It sits in the inner rather than the outer membrane

explanation.summary: Meningococcal endotoxin is a lipooligosaccharide because it lacks the O antigen found in typical gram-negative lipopolysaccharide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typical lipopolysaccharide has three parts: lipid A (the toxic component), a core polysaccharide, and an O antigen. N. meningitidis omits the O antigen, producing the shorter lipooligosaccharide. It still functions as an endotoxin, triggering immunologic responses and a potential cytokine storm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is a structural membrane endotoxin, not a secreted exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipid A is retained and is precisely what makes the molecule toxic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The core polysaccharide remains; it is the O antigen that is missing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The molecule remains an outer membrane component, as in other gram-negative organisms.

questions.stem: The polysaccharide capsule of N. meningitidis carries the antigens used to divide the species into serogroups. Which of the following groups includes the most common pathogenic serogroups?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serogroups a, b, c, d, e, and f

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serogroups A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serogroups D, E, F, G, H, and I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serogroups I, II, III, IV, V, and VI

explanation.summary: Capsular antigens define meningococcal serogroups A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135 as the most common pathogenic groups.
explanation.whyCorrect: Specific antigens within the polysaccharide capsule determine the serogroup. A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135 account for the pathogenic strains, with B, C, Y, and W-135 the most common causes of disease and serogroup A notable for causing epidemics. Vaccines are directed at these capsular antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Numeric designations are not used for meningococcal capsular serogroups.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lowercase serotypes a through f describe encapsulated H. influenzae, not N. meningitidis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These letters are not the recognized pathogenic meningococcal serogroups.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Roman numeral designations are not used for meningococcal capsular serogroups.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl received the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) at her last visit. Her mother asks whether any pathogenic meningococcal serogroup remains uncovered by that vaccine. Which of the following serogroups requires a separate vaccine?

explanation.summary: MenACWY does not protect against serogroup B, which requires a separate recombinant protein vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The quadrivalent conjugate vaccine covers serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y but not B. A separate recombinant protein vaccine against serogroup B is available in the United States for children 10 years of age and older. A pentavalent product, MenABCWY, covers all five serogroups in one vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serogroup A is one of the four serogroups included in MenACWY.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serogroup C is included in the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serogroup W-135 is the W component of MenACWY.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serogroup Y is the Y component of MenACWY.

questions.stem: A healthy child is seen for a routine health maintenance visit, and the parents ask when the meningococcal conjugate vaccine series should begin. Routine vaccination is recommended starting at which of the following ages, with a booster at 16 years?

explanation.summary: Routine meningococcal conjugate vaccination is given at 11 to 12 years of age with a booster at age 16.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjugated vaccines developed against meningococcal capsular antigens are recommended for adolescents at 11 to 12 years, followed by a booster at 16 years. This timing precedes the second disease peak at 18 to 25 years, when close quarters such as dormitories and military camps increase risk. By contrast, H. influenzae type b vaccination begins at 2 months of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two months is when the Hib series begins, not meningococcal vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ages 4 to 6 years fall before the recommended adolescent start.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve months is earlier than the recommended start of routine meningococcal vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting until 18 to 21 years would leave adolescents unprotected through the rising-risk years.

questions.stem: N. meningitidis first establishes itself by binding nonciliated nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, endothelium, and erythrocytes. Which of the following pairs of surface structures mediates this attachment?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opacity proteins and type IV pili

explanation.summary: Opacity proteins and type IV pili are the attachment and invasion factors of N. meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opacity proteins allow the organism to adhere to human cells, and type IV pili bind nonciliated nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, endothelium, and erythrocytes. The pili also aggregate bacteria into units that move across the surface by twitching motility. These adhesins are the first step toward colonization and later invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cord factor is a mycobacterial lipid and is not an adhesin of this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: N. meningitidis is nonmotile and has no flagella; M protein is a streptococcal factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoteichoic acid is a gram-positive wall component and mycolic acid is found in mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein A and coagulase are staphylococcal virulence factors.

questions.stem: After N. meningitidis pili aggregate the bacteria into units that migrate across the nasopharyngeal surface by twitching motility, the organism binds host cell microvilli. Which of the following best describes what happens next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enters in vesicles and spreads to adjacent cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forms spores that persist within the mucosal layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: It multiplies only inside erythrocytes after lysing them

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes an exotoxin that lyses cells from the outside

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stays extracellular and is rapidly cleared by neutrophils

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis is a facultative intracellular organism that enters cells in membrane-bound vesicles and destroys them as it spreads.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial units bind microvilli and enter the cell inside membrane-bound vesicles. Once intracellular, the organism migrates through the cytoplasm into adjacent cells, destroying them in the process. This facultative intracellular lifestyle also lets it reside within polymorphonuclear leukocytes, which is why it is seen inside neutrophils on smears.

whyWrongByChoice.B: N. meningitidis does not form spores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It binds erythrocytes but does not replicate exclusively within them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its principal toxin is the membrane-bound lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, not a secreted cytolytic exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The organism survives inside polymorphonuclear leukocytes rather than being simply cleared by them.

questions.stem: Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae colonize the nasopharynx in part by degrading the antibody that guards mucosal surfaces. Which of the following virulence factors is responsible?

explanation.summary: IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA and allows both organisms to colonize the nasopharynx.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA is the dominant immunoglobulin at mucosal surfaces. Both N. meningitidis and H. influenzae produce an IgA protease that cleaves it, which is why each can establish nasopharyngeal colonization. S. pneumoniae, the third major cause of acute meningitis, also produces this enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipooligosaccharide acts as an endotoxin that drives inflammation rather than cleaving IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opacity proteins mediate attachment to human cells, not antibody destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The capsule blocks phagocytosis and complement but does not degrade antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV pili bind epithelium, endothelium, and erythrocytes but have no protease activity.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is admitted with his third episode of meningococcal disease in 4 years. He has no history of splenectomy, and immunoglobulin levels and a neutrophil count are normal. Total hemolytic activity measured by CH50 is undetectable. Which of the following deficiencies best explains his recurrent infections?

explanation.summary: Deficiency of the terminal complement proteins C5 through C9 prevents membrane attack complex formation and predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Host defense against N. meningitidis depends on antibodies (IgM, IgG, and IgA) together with the complement cascade, which mediates bacterial lysis. When the terminal pathway proteins C5 through C9 are deficient, the membrane attack complex cannot be assembled, and the risk and severity of meningococcal disease rise sharply. The undetectable CH50 with normal immunoglobulins and neutrophils points to that terminal pathway defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic granulomatous disease is a defect of the neutrophil oxidative burst, with intact complement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs leukocyte migration and leaves complement activity normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase deficiency affects neutrophil killing and would not abolish complement activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective IgA deficiency involves antibody rather than complement, and immunoglobulin levels here are normal.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with sickle cell anemia and documented autosplenectomy develops fulminant meningococcal sepsis. Which of the following best explains her heightened susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clearance of encapsulated organisms is impaired

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement proteins are consumed during hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mucociliary clearance of the airway is reduced

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils cannot generate an oxidative burst

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory antibody is cleaved at the mucosal surface

explanation.summary: The spleen is a key defense against encapsulated organisms, so asplenic patients are prone to severe meningococcal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic macrophages clear encapsulated bacteria from the bloodstream. Repeated thrombosis, fibrosis, and necrosis in chronic sickle cell anemia produce autosplenectomy, leaving the patient functionally asplenic. Infections with encapsulated organisms, including the encapsulated N. meningitidis, are therefore common and often severe in these patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sickle cell hemolysis does not deplete the complement cascade as the mechanism of risk here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced mucociliary clearance is a risk factor in smoking, COPD, and cystic fibrosis, not asplenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An oxidative burst defect describes chronic granulomatous disease, not autosplenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cleavage of IgA is a bacterial virulence strategy rather than a consequence of losing the spleen.

questions.stem: A public health officer is counseling contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis about how the organism spreads. Which of the following is the mode of transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite of an infected arthropod vector

explanation.summary: N. meningitidis spreads person to person by inhalation of respiratory droplets; humans are the only natural host.
explanation.whyCorrect: Humans are the sole natural reservoir, and the organism lives in the respiratory tract. Transmission occurs when respiratory droplets are inhaled, after which the bacteria enter the nasopharynx and may become transient members of the microbiota without causing symptoms. From there they can progress into the upper respiratory tract, although they less often invade the lower tract.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No arthropod vector transmits N. meningitidis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans are the only natural host, so there is no animal reservoir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no waterborne route for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bloodborne percutaneous spread is not how this organism is acquired.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college freshman living in a dormitory is hospitalized with meningococcal meningitis. She is the second case in that dormitory this month, although no student reports contact with a sick person. Which of the following best accounts for the clustering of cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymptomatic carriers spread it in closely quartered groups

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contaminated food in the dining hall spreads the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Latent infection reactivates under periods of stress

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shared bathroom water supplies harbor the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism persists for weeks on environmental surfaces

explanation.summary: Outbreaks occur in closely quartered populations because asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriers shed the organism in respiratory droplets.
explanation.whyCorrect: People can carry N. meningitidis asymptomatically in the nasopharynx, and carriers spread it by respiratory droplets to produce new carriers or disease in those without antibodies against the strain. Community outbreaks are therefore common in college dormitories, military camps, and religious pilgrimages. The 18 to 25 year age range is also one of the two epidemiologic peaks of community-acquired disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no foodborne route of meningococcal transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disease follows transmission or progression from carriage, not reactivation of latency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The organism is not waterborne.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spread is person to person by droplets rather than through durable environmental contamination.

questions.stem: In meningococcal disease, bacteremia precedes invasion of the central nervous system. Which of the following structures is the usual point of entry into the central nervous system, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The arachnoid granulations, because they reabsorb the CSF

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood-brain barrier, because tight junctions are absent

choices.label: C
choices.text: The choroid plexus, because its blood flow rate is high

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dural venous sinuses, because blood flow is sluggish

choices.label: E
choices.text: The olfactory epithelium, because it abuts the meninges

explanation.summary: Bacteremic N. meningitidis reaches the central nervous system at the choroid plexus, which has a high rate of blood flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: After bacteremia develops, the organism is carried to the choroid plexus, where the high blood flow rate makes it an accessible entry point. Invasion of the central nervous system triggers cytokine release and inflammation, clots form in vessels, and leukocytes leak out to produce pus around the meninges.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arachnoid granulations reabsorb cerebrospinal fluid but are not the described portal of entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The blood-brain barrier is defined by tight junctions, which are present rather than absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sluggish sinus flow is not the reason given for central nervous system seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Entry is hematogenous from bacteremia rather than direct extension across olfactory epithelium.

questions.stem: A clinician is reviewing the presenting features of meningococcal meningitis and notes that one symptom is reported by about 84% of patients, more than any other. Which of the following symptoms is it?

explanation.summary: Severe headache is the single most common symptom of meningococcal meningitis, occurring in about 84% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the common presenting symptoms, severe headache is reported in roughly 84% of cases. Fever above 38 C and stiff neck each occur in about 74%, and nausea in about 62%. Seizures, coma, and rash are recognized but less common manifestations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fever above 38 C occurs in about 74% of patients, less often than headache.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nausea occurs in about 62% of patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seizures fall among the less common symptoms, along with coma and rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stiff neck is also reported in about 74% of patients.

questions.stem: The classic triad of acute bacterial meningitis consists of fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Approximately what proportion of patients present with all three findings?

explanation.summary: About 41% of patients with acute bacterial meningitis present with all three elements of the classic triad, although most have at least two.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of fever, nuchal rigidity, and a sudden change in mental status is classic but incomplete in most patients. Roughly 41% show all three, while the majority present with at least two of the three. Additional symptoms such as headache, nausea, seizures, coma, and rash may accompany them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates how often the full triad appears.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One quarter is below the reported proportion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One third is close but below the reported figure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 74% corresponds to the frequency of fever or stiff neck individually, not the complete triad.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with meningococcal septicemia becomes hypotensive and does not respond to fluids or pressors. Imaging demonstrates bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, and cortisol is undetectable. Which of the following best describes this complication?

explanation.summary: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is adrenal hemorrhage and necrosis with adrenal failure during meningococcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Meningococcemia is a bloodstream infection in which endotoxin release drives high fever, hemorrhagic rash, perivascular infiltration, and thrombosis of small vessels. N. meningitidis is notorious for causing Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, in which adrenal hemorrhage and necrosis leave the glands unable to make the hormones needed to maintain systemic organ function, producing refractory shock.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an ascending demyelinating polyneuropathy without adrenal involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolytic uremic syndrome causes renal failure with hemolysis and does not destroy the adrenal glands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a facial palsy with vesicles caused by varicella-zoster reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary infarction, not adrenal hemorrhage during sepsis.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with meningococcemia has spreading purpura and gangrenous changes of the toes. Laboratory studies show prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, a low fibrinogen level, and thrombocytopenia. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of platelets in the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial cleavage of von Willebrand factor multimers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumption of clotting factors with small-vessel thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow failure from bacterial invasion of the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency caused by broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation.summary: Meningococcal endotoxin triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation, which consumes coagulation factors and causes small-vessel thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endotoxin release in meningococcemia leads to perivascular infiltration and thrombosis of small blood vessels. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is characterized by consumption of coagulation factors, which produces circulatory instability and collapse. Clinically this shows as a hemorrhagic rash with petechiae, purpura, and digital gangrene alongside the abnormal coagulation studies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune platelet destruction would not prolong clotting times or lower fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleavage of von Willebrand factor multimers is not a described meningococcal mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow invasion is not the described mechanism of coagulopathy in this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency does not explain thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, or gangrene.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, and the cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following additional findings is most characteristic of this organism rather than of Haemophilus influenzae?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thumbprint sign on lateral neck x-ray

explanation.summary: Petechiae, purpura, and digital gangrene reflect meningococcemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation, a hallmark of N. meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Simultaneous infection of the central nervous system and blood is common with N. meningitidis. The bloodstream component, meningococcemia, produces a hemorrhagic rash with petechiae and purpura and can progress to digital gangrene through small-vessel thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Rash is a recognized, if less common, symptom accompanying meningococcal meningitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cherry-red, edematous epiglottis is the examination finding in Hib epiglottitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drooling with a muffled cough describes acute epiglottitis caused by H. influenzae type b.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tender reddish-blue facial swelling describes the cellulitis caused by Hib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thumbprint sign is the radiographic finding of the thickened epiglottis in Hib epiglottitis.

questions.stem: A hospital committee is reviewing empiric therapy for suspected meningococcal disease. Which of the following statements about antimicrobial treatment of N. meningitidis is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resistance is now widespread, so vancomycin is required

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resistance is rare, and ceftriaxone remains effective first

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism is intrinsically resistant to all beta-lactams

choices.label: D
choices.text: Therapy should be delayed until susceptibilities return

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated cases resolve without significant complications

explanation.summary: Meningococcal resistance to common agents is rare, and ceftriaxone remains generally effective as a first agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reports of beta-lactamase production and altered penicillin-binding proteins exist, but resistance against common antimicrobial agents is rare. Ceftriaxone is generally effective as a first agent. Susceptibility testing still matters because inadequately treated and untreated cases carry high mortality, and strong broad-spectrum agents should be used sparingly to limit future resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance is rare rather than widespread, so vancomycin is not required for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism is not intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams; ceftriaxone works.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delaying therapy is dangerous because untreated cases have high mortality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Untreated meningococcal disease carries high mortality rather than resolving spontaneously.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant who has received no childhood vaccinations is admitted with fever, lethargy, and a bulging fontanelle. Gram stain of the cerebrospinal fluid shows small gram-negative organisms intermediate in shape between cocci and bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: H. influenzae is a gram-negative coccobacillus and a classic cause of meningitis in unvaccinated infants and children.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. influenzae is a nonmotile, nonhemolytic, fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus whose shape is intermediate between a coccus and a bacillus. It is another cause of acute purulent meningitis, and its clinical presentation is indistinct from meningitis caused by other bacteria such as N. meningitidis. Disease is most common in unvaccinated infants and children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a frank gram-negative bacillus rather than a coccobacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N. meningitidis appears as a gram-negative diplococcus, not a coccobacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive organism and would stain purple.

questions.stem: A laboratory is preparing media to culture H. influenzae from a sputum specimen. This organism is fastidious and requires supplementation with which of the following?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mannitol and a high salt concentration

explanation.summary: H. influenzae requires factor X (hematin) and factor V (NAD), both found inside erythrocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: As a fastidious organism, H. influenzae will not grow unless both factor V (NAD) and factor X (hematin) are available. Because these factors are contained in red blood cells, the organism must be grown on media enriched with lysed blood or blood products. Chocolate agar, in which heating has lysed the erythrocytes, supplies both.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholesterol requirement is not a feature of this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cysteine and iron supplementation are requirements of other fastidious organisms, not H. influenzae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannitol with high salt describes a selective medium for staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine and biotin are not the named growth factors for H. influenzae.

questions.stem: A respiratory specimen is plated on sheep blood agar that is also streaked with Staphylococcus aureus. After incubation, tiny colonies appear only in a band immediately adjacent to the staphylococcal growth. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The staphylococci acidify the agar, enhancing its growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: The staphylococci chelate host transferrin to supply iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: The staphylococci generate carbon dioxide needed for growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: The staphylococci lyse red cells, releasing X and V factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: The staphylococci secrete a beta-lactamase that protects it

explanation.summary: The satellite phenomenon occurs when beta-hemolytic bacteria lyse red cells and release the X and V factors that H. influenzae needs.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. influenzae cannot grow on plain blood agar because it cannot lyse the erythrocytes itself. When a beta-hemolytic organism such as S. aureus is present, its hemolysis frees factor X (hematin) and factor V (NAD) into the surrounding agar. H. influenzae therefore grows only in that vicinity, a pattern known as the satellite phenomenon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acidification of the medium does not account for the localized growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron chelation from transferrin is not the mechanism behind satellite colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although carbon dioxide can aid fastidious organisms, the satellite pattern reflects release of X and V factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-lactamase protection is irrelevant on a plate with no beta-lactam antibiotic.

questions.stem: A technologist notes that a pure culture of H. influenzae fails to grow when plated on unsupplemented sheep blood agar, yet grows well on chocolate agar. Which of the following best explains the failure on blood agar?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot lyse red cells to obtain the X and V factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is inhibited by the sodium chloride in the medium

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is lysed by complement proteins in the sheep blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires an anaerobic atmosphere that plates lack

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires bile salts that blood agar does not contain

explanation.summary: H. influenzae cannot grow on blood agar because it lacks the ability to lyse erythrocytes and free the X and V factors inside them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factors X (hematin) and V (NAD) sit within intact red blood cells. H. influenzae is nonhemolytic and cannot rupture those cells, so on plain blood agar the nutrients remain unavailable. Chocolate agar solves the problem because heating has already lysed the erythrocytes and released both factors into the medium.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood agar is not a high-salt medium, and salt inhibition is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure to grow reflects missing nutrients, not complement-mediated lysis in the plate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The organism does not require an anaerobic atmosphere to grow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bile salts are components of selective enteric media and are not a growth requirement here.

questions.stem: Encapsulated strains of H. influenzae are classified by the antigen present in the capsule. Which of the following correctly describes this classification and the strain responsible for most fulminant disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four serotypes, a to d, with type d most fulminant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nine serotypes, a to i, with type f most fulminant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Six serotypes, 1 to 6, with type 3 most fulminant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Six serotypes, a to f, with type b most fulminant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three serotypes, a to c, with type a most fulminant

explanation.summary: Encapsulated H. influenzae comprises six serotypes, a through f, and type b (Hib) causes most fulminant disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The capsule lets the organism evade immune attack and bind factors that downregulate immunologic cascades. Encapsulated subspecies are divided into six serotypes, a through f, based on the capsular antigen. Type b, abbreviated Hib, is the most common cause of fulminant disease and is the target of the conjugate vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There are six serotypes, not four, and type b rather than type d is the fulminant strain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There are six lettered serotypes, and type b is the one responsible for fulminant disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotypes are lettered a through f rather than numbered.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three serotypes understates the classification, and type a is not the fulminant strain.

questions.stem: A student is comparing nasopharyngeal carriage rates for encapsulated type b and nonencapsulated strains of H. influenzae. Which of the following best represents those carrier rates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type b, 50% to 80%; nonencapsulated, less than 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type b, about 90%; nonencapsulated, less than 1%

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type b, less than 5%; nonencapsulated, 10% to 15%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type b, less than 5%; nonencapsulated, 50% to 80%

explanation.summary: The carrier rate of Hib is less than 5%, while nonencapsular subtypes are carried by 50% to 80% of people.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. influenzae is normal flora of the nasopharyngeal tract, but the two groups are carried at very different rates. Fewer than 5% of people carry type b, whereas nonencapsular subtypes are carried by 50% to 80%. Why the organism transitions from carriage to invasion of deeper tissues is unknown.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The figures are reversed; the encapsulated type b strain is carried far less often.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Equal carriage rates do not reflect the marked difference between the two groups.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type b carriage is uncommon rather than near universal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The type b figure is right, but nonencapsulated carriage is far higher than 10% to 15%.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy who has received no routine childhood vaccinations is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of sore throat and a temperature of 39.5 C (103.1 F). He is drooling, swallowing is difficult, and his oxygen saturation is 92%. Lateral neck radiography shows a thickened epiglottis. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: H. influenzae type b is the most common cause of acute epiglottitis, a medical emergency in unvaccinated children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hib is the most common etiologic agent of acute epiglottitis, and the inflamed epiglottis can obstruct the airway. Onset is sudden, with fever, sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, muffled cough, and hoarseness that can progress to respiratory compromise. Lack of vaccination is what puts this child at acute risk, and the thickened epiglottis produces the thumbprint sign on radiography.

whyWrongByChoice.B: M. catarrhalis is a cause of acute otitis media, not epiglottitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N. meningitidis causes meningitis and meningococcemia rather than epiglottitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is a common cause of pneumonia to a lesser extent but is not the leading cause of epiglottitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis, among other infections, rather than classic epiglottitis.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old unvaccinated girl presents with sudden fever, drooling, muffled voice, and stridor, and acute epiglottitis is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give oral corticosteroids and discharge with follow-up

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a throat swab for culture before starting therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform direct laryngoscopy in the examination room

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the neck radiograph in 6 hours to confirm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secure the airway, then begin antibiotic therapy

explanation.summary: Airway protection comes first in acute epiglottitis, followed by antibiotic therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency because the inflamed epiglottis can obstruct the airway, and without prompt treatment patients can progress to complete obstruction and death. The initial step in treatment is airway protection together with antibiotic therapy. Direct examination should be avoided when possible, since a swab or contact can trigger laryngospasm and obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Discharging a child at risk of airway obstruction would be dangerous.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Swabbing the pharynx risks triggering laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct examination should be avoided for the same reason, particularly outside a controlled setting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delaying definitive management for repeat imaging risks fatal airway compromise.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy who completed the full Hib vaccine series has his third episode of acute otitis media this year. Middle ear fluid culture grows H. influenzae. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The child most likely has a terminal complement defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: The infection is caused by a nonencapsulated strain

choices.label: C
choices.text: The strain switched to a capsule type not in the vaccine

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vaccine failed because it was given before 6 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vaccine protects only after a booster at age 5 years

explanation.summary: The Hib vaccine covers only capsular type b, so nonencapsulated strains still cause otitis media, sinusitis, and conjunctivitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonencapsulated strains of H. influenzae invade locally in the respiratory tract and cause non-fulminant infections such as acute otitis media, sinusitis, and conjunctivitis. The conjugate vaccine is directed at the type b capsular antigen and so does not protect against most of these infections. Vaccinated children can therefore still have recurrent otitis media caused by nonencapsulated strains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement deficiency is associated with severe Neisseria disease, not routine otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-fulminant ear infections are typically caused by nonencapsulated strains rather than a switched capsule type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vaccine timing does not explain infection by strains the vaccine never covered.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protection does not hinge on a booster at 5 years; the limitation is coverage of type b only.

questions.stem: A pediatrician reviews the bacterial causes of acute otitis media, noting that all of them are normal flora of the nasopharynx. Which of the following groups lists the most common causes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, and M. catarrhalis

choices.label: B
choices.text: L. monocytogenes, S. aureus, and S. pneumoniae

choices.label: C
choices.text: N. meningitidis, S. aureus, and P. aeruginosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: P. aeruginosa, M. catarrhalis, and S. pyogenes

choices.label: E
choices.text: S. pyogenes, E. coli, and K. pneumoniae

explanation.summary: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, and M. catarrhalis are the most common bacterial causes of acute otitis media.
explanation.whyCorrect: These three organisms are the leading bacterial causes of acute otitis media, and all three are normal flora of the nasopharynx. That colonization is what allows them to reach the middle ear when normal clearing mechanisms fail. For H. influenzae, this form of disease is typically caused by nonencapsulated strains.

whyWrongByChoice.B: L. monocytogenes is a foodborne pathogen and is not a common cause of otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N. meningitidis and P. aeruginosa are not among the leading causes of acute otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. aeruginosa and S. pyogenes do not belong with M. catarrhalis in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes, E. coli, and K. pneumoniae are not the classic otitis media trio.

questions.stem: The Hib vaccine links the capsular polysaccharide of H. influenzae type b to inactivated tetanus toxoid. Which of the following best explains why this conjugation is necessary?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It broadens coverage to all six capsular serotypes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inactivates the bacteria before the antigen is given

choices.label: C
choices.text: It recruits T cell help for a T-independent antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shields the polysaccharide from bacterial IgA protease

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies passive antibody that acts immediately

explanation.summary: Conjugating the capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier recruits T cell help, converting a T-independent antigen into one that generates durable immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsular polysaccharides such as the Hib antigen are T-independent antigens and by themselves induce a weak, short-lived response. Covalently binding the polysaccharide to a protein, typically inactivated tetanus toxoid, elicits T cell help. Immunity against Hib then depends on anticapsular antibodies working together with a functional complement system, and this vaccine has reduced invasive disease by 99%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vaccine covers only serotype b, not all six capsular serotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaccine contains a purified capsular antigen rather than whole bacteria requiring inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protection from IgA protease is not the purpose of conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaccine induces active immunity; passive antibody comes from transplacental transfer.

questions.stem: A pediatric resident notes that invasive H. influenzae infection has a peak incidence within a narrow age window. Which of the following identifies that window and the best explanation for it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 11 to 12 years, as vaccine immunity wanes then

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 to 5 years, as day care exposure peaks then

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 to 18 months, as transplacental antibodies wane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Over 65 years, as immunosenescence reduces antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: The newborn period, as no maternal antibody crosses

explanation.summary: Invasive H. influenzae infection peaks at 6 to 18 months, after transplacental antibodies wane but before vaccination has taken effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Passive immunity from transplacental antibodies protects infants until vaccination. The peak incidence of infection falls at 6 to 18 months, when those maternal antibodies have declined but the child has not yet been immunized. As active antibodies accumulate through adolescence and adulthood and through vaccines, systemic Hib infection becomes rare.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age 11 to 12 years is the start of routine meningococcal vaccination, not the Hib peak.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infections occur in this age range, but the peak incidence is earlier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rates do rise again in the elderly, but the described peak incidence is in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Newborns are protected by transplacental antibodies rather than being at peak risk.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had three episodes of H. influenzae bronchitis in the past year. Which of the following conditions in his history would most likely have predisposed him by reducing mucociliary clearance?

explanation.summary: Reduced mucociliary clearance, as in cystic fibrosis, smoking, and COPD, is a major risk factor for H. influenzae respiratory infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: H. influenzae is normal flora of the nasopharynx and causes disease when clearing mechanisms fail. Reduced mucociliary clearance is a specific named risk factor and occurs in smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and cystic fibrosis. Nonencapsulated strains in particular invade locally when a concurrent infection or structural damage prevents normal respiratory tract clearing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA deficiency is an antibody defect and does not reduce ciliary clearance of the airway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asplenia impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms from the blood rather than mucociliary function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Terminal complement deficiency raises the risk of severe Neisseria disease and does not impair ciliary clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diabetes is not the mechanism of impaired mucociliary clearance described for this organism.

questions.stem: A hospital microbiology laboratory receives several gram-negative bacillary isolates from urine, blood, and stool cultures. All of them grow well on MacConkey agar, but the technologist notes that they differ from one another in motility, urease activity, and the speed with which they turn the medium pink. Which property is shared by all members of the Enterobacteriaceae family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They all ferment glucose to acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: They all hydrolyze urea to ammonia

choices.label: D
choices.text: They all produce hydrogen sulfide on TSI agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are all motile by means of flagella

explanation.summary: Every member of the Enterobacteriaceae ferments glucose; lactose fermentation, motility, urease, and H2S are what separate the genera.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose fermentation is the common denominator of the family, which is why the differential media used for these organisms focus on lactose rather than glucose. MacConkey agar separates the family into lactose fermenters and non-fermenters, and additional tests such as motility, urease, and H2S production narrow the identification to a genus. This is the basis of the gram-negative lab algorithm used to work up an enteric isolate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Proteus, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia do not turn MacConkey pink, and Citrobacter ferments lactose only slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. coli and Serratia are urease negative, which helps separate them from Proteus and Klebsiella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only Salmonella, Proteus, and Citrobacter produce H2S; E. coli and K. pneumoniae do not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Klebsiella and Shigella are nonmotile and grow only along the stab line in a motility tube.

questions.stem: A gram-negative bacillus isolated from a hospitalized patient's urine produces colorless colonies on MacConkey agar at 24 hours, but by 72 hours the colonies and surrounding medium have taken on a faint pink color. The isolate is motile, urease positive, blackens the butt of a TSI tube, and produces no pigment. Which organism is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Citrobacter is a slow lactose fermenter that is motile, urease positive, and produces H2S.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fast lactose fermenters change the color of MacConkey agar within 24 to 48 hours, while slow fermenters take beyond 48 hours and produce a less intense pink. Citrobacter is one of the slow fermenters, and it is additionally motile, urease positive, and an H2S producer. That combination distinguishes it from the other common enteric genera.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a fast lactose fermenter that is urease negative and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is a fast lactose fermenter, is nonmotile, and forms mucoid colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus does not ferment lactose at all, so its colonies remain colorless indefinitely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia is urease negative and produces the red pigment prodigiosin.

questions.stem: A stool specimen is plated onto eosin methylene blue (EMB) agar. After overnight incubation, the technologist reports colonies with a striking green metallic sheen. Which organism is most likely present?

explanation.summary: A green metallic sheen on EMB agar is the classic appearance of E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: EMB agar contains eosin and methylene blue, which inhibit gram-positive organisms and stain lactose-fermenting bacteria black. E. coli is the exception: it interacts with the dyes to form colonies with a characteristic green metallic sheen. This finding is used together with lactose fermentation and beta-hemolysis to identify E. coli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter ferments lactose slowly and does not develop a metallic sheen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterobacter ferments lactose and stains black on EMB like the other fermenters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella ferments lactose and therefore appears black on EMB, not metallic green.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella does not ferment lactose, so it forms colorless colonies on this medium.

questions.stem: A urine culture from a patient with a long-term indwelling catheter grows a gram-negative rod that spreads across the plate in concentric waves rather than as discrete colonies. The isolate produces colorless colonies on MacConkey agar, is strongly urease positive, and blackens the butt of a TSI tube. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Swarming motility with urease and H2S production in a non-lactose fermenter identifies Proteus mirabilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteus mirabilis is motile in a unique swarming pattern that spreads over the agar surface. It does not ferment lactose, it is urease positive, and it is one of the enteric organisms that produces H2S on TSI agar. This triad separates it from the other genera in the family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli ferments lactose, is urease negative, and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is nonmotile with mucoid colonies and does not produce H2S.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia is urease negative and produces red pigment rather than swarming growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella is nonmotile and does not produce H2S on TSI agar.

questions.stem: Sputum from a patient with pneumonia grows a gram-negative rod that forms large, glistening, mucoid colonies. The organism turns MacConkey agar deep pink within 24 hours, shows no migration away from the stab in a motility tube, and is urease positive. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Mucoid colonies from a nonmotile, urease-positive fast lactose fermenter point to Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Klebsiella pneumoniae ferments lactose rapidly, so MacConkey agar turns pink within 24 to 48 hours. It is one of only two enteric organisms in this group that are nonmotile, and it is urease positive. Its mucoid colonies reflect its abundant capsule and are a recognized clue on the plate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter is motile and only weakly urease positive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is motile, urease negative, and shows a green sheen on EMB rather than mucoid growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus does not ferment lactose and displays swarming motility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella does not ferment lactose and is motile.

questions.stem: An intensive care unit isolate from a respiratory specimen is a motile gram-negative rod whose colonies develop a deep red pigment after incubation at room temperature. The organism is urease negative. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Red prodigiosin pigment from a motile, urease-negative enteric rod identifies Serratia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serratia species produce the red pigment prodigiosin, which is their single most recognizable laboratory feature. They are motile and urease negative, which separates them from Proteus, Klebsiella, and Citrobacter. Serratia is one of the enteric opportunists that becomes prominent in hospitalized patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter is urease positive and produces no pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli produces no pigment and shows a green metallic sheen on EMB agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is nonmotile and urease positive, and its colonies are mucoid rather than red.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is urease positive, produces H2S, and swarms across the plate.

questions.stem: A laboratory performs motility testing by stabbing several enteric isolates into tubes of solid agar. Two of the isolates grow only along the narrow inoculation tract, while the rest cloud the surrounding agar. Which pair of organisms is expected to remain confined to the stab line?

explanation.summary: Among the enteric organisms, Klebsiella and Shigella are the nonmotile ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Motility is tested by piercing solid agar in a test tube; motile organisms migrate beyond the inoculated area and cloud the medium, while nonmotile organisms stay within the tract. E. coli, Salmonella, Serratia, Proteus, and some Citrobacter are motile. Klebsiella and Shigella lack this ability and therefore produce growth only along the stab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both E. coli and Salmonella are motile and will cloud the agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proteus is not only motile but swarms, and Serratia is motile as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella is motile, and at least some Citrobacter isolates are motile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia and E. coli are both motile organisms.

questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with fever and diarrhea is inoculated onto triple sugar iron (TSI) agar. After incubation, the butt of the tube has turned black. Which organism is most consistent with this result?

explanation.summary: Blackening of TSI agar indicates H2S production, which among these organisms only Salmonella performs.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI agar contains sodium thiosulfate and ferrous sulfate, and H2S produced by the organism reacts with the iron salt to deposit black ferrous sulfide. Salmonella, Proteus, and Citrobacter are the H2S producers in this family. The gram-negative lab algorithm uses this step to separate Salmonella and Proteus from Shigella and Yersinia among the non-lactose fermenters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli does not produce H2S, so the butt of the tube would not blacken.
whyWrongByChoice.B: K. pneumoniae is explicitly H2S negative and also ferments lactose rapidly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella falls on the H2S-negative branch of the enteric algorithm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia is also an H2S-negative non-lactose fermenter.

questions.stem: A student examines a TSI tube in which the deep portion of the medium has become jet black after overnight incubation of an enteric isolate. Which chemical reaction accounts for this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gas produced by fermentation darkens the agar as it cracks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen sulfide reacts with ferrous sulfate to form ferrous sulfide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phenol red is reduced to a dark pigment under acidic conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prodigiosin made by the organism diffuses through the agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urease hydrolyzes urea and alkalinizes the deep part of the tube

explanation.summary: The black color of TSI agar is insoluble ferrous sulfide precipitated from bacterial H2S.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI agar contains sodium thiosulfate as a sulfur source and ferrous sulfate as an indicator. Organisms that reduce thiosulfate generate H2S, which reacts with the ferrous salt to form ferrous sulfide, an insoluble black precipitate. Sugar fermentation, gas production, and H2S production are read together to separate members of the family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gas production is read as cracks or bubbles in the agar, not as a color change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenol red is the pH indicator in TSI and turns yellow with acid, never black.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prodigiosin is the red pigment of Serratia and has nothing to do with the TSI reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urease activity is tested separately and does not generate a black precipitate.

questions.stem: An enteric isolate is inoculated onto TSI agar. Before inoculation the medium is red; after incubation both the slant and the butt of the tube are bright yellow. What does this color change indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism fermented one or more sugars to acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism hydrolyzed urea and raised the pH

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism is nonmotile and stayed along the stab

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism produced gas that cracked the agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produced hydrogen sulfide from thiosulfate

explanation.summary: Yellow TSI agar means a sugar was fermented and the resulting acid turned phenol red yellow.
explanation.whyCorrect: TSI contains lactose, sucrose, and glucose along with phenol red, a pH-sensitive dye that gives the medium its red color. When any of these sugars is fermented, the environment becomes acidic and phenol red turns yellow. Reading the slant and the butt separately shows which sugars were used.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alkalinization would move phenol red away from yellow, not toward it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Motility is assessed in a separate soft agar tube, not by TSI color.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gas production is read as cracks or bubbles within the agar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H2S production is signaled by a black precipitate, not by a yellow color.

questions.stem: A blood agar plate inoculated with an enteric gram-negative rod shows a zone of complete clearing of the red blood cells around the colonies. Among the common members of Enterobacteriaceae, which organism is expected to produce this pattern?

explanation.summary: E. coli is the only beta-hemolytic organism among the Enterobacteriaceae discussed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete clearing of red cells around a colony is beta-hemolysis. Of the enteric organisms covered, only E. coli is beta-hemolytic on blood agar. Because the rest of the family is not hemolytic, hemolysis patterns are otherwise not used to distinguish between members of Enterobacteriaceae.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is not beta-hemolytic; it is recognized by mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proteus is not beta-hemolytic; its clue on agar is swarming growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia is not beta-hemolytic; its clue is red prodigiosin pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella is not beta-hemolytic and forms colorless colonies on MacConkey agar.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man develops fever, hypotension, and tachypnea 12 hours after a gram-negative rod is recovered from his blood. Cytokine-driven systemic inflammation is thought to be responsible for his presentation. Which bacterial component is the principal trigger of this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fimbriae used for attachment to host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flagellar H antigen on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptidoglycan of the inner cell wall layer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polysaccharide K1 capsule of the organism

explanation.summary: LPS in the gram-negative outer membrane is the endotoxin that drives inflammation and sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A major virulence factor of gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, is the LPS found in the outer membrane of the cell wall. LPS is notorious for provoking inflammatory responses that can progress to sepsis. Its three parts are the O-specific polysaccharide, the core polysaccharide, and lipid A.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fimbriae mediate attachment to host surfaces rather than systemic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The H antigen is a flagellar protein used for strain typing, not an endotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is a structural component and is not the endotoxin described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The K1 capsule promotes immune evasion in neonatal meningitis, not endotoxic shock.

questions.stem: A patient with gram-negative bacteremia is given an appropriate bactericidal antibiotic. Within hours his fever spikes higher and his blood pressure falls further, even though repeat cultures show that the organism is being cleared. Which mechanism best explains this paradoxical worsening?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Destruction of the bacteria releases more LPS into the body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shiga-like toxin is released and shuts down hepatic protein synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surviving organisms upregulate fimbriae and invade the bloodstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibiotic is directly toxic to vascular smooth muscle cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism switches to an H antigen the immune system cannot see

explanation.summary: Killing gram-negative bacteria liberates LPS, which can transiently intensify the inflammatory response.
explanation.whyCorrect: LPS sits in the outer membrane, so destroying the organism releases more of it into the circulation. That additional endotoxin further fuels the inflammatory cascade even as the bacterial burden falls. This is why treating a gram-negative infection can temporarily exacerbate the immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Shiga-like toxin is an EHEC product acting on enterocytes and glomerular endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fimbriae mediate attachment and are not upregulated as a response to antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Direct antibiotic toxicity to vessels is not the mechanism taught for this phenomenon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H antigens are used for strain typing and are not switched to evade therapy.

questions.stem: A microbiology lecture diagrams the lipopolysaccharide molecule of a gram-negative bacillus from the surface of the organism inward. Which set of structures makes up this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Core polysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, and fimbrial protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipid A, flagellin protein, and capsular polysaccharide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipoteichoic acid, core polysaccharide, and mycolic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: O-specific polysaccharide, core polysaccharide, and lipid A

choices.label: E
choices.text: O-specific polysaccharide, peptidoglycan, and porin protein

explanation.summary: LPS has three parts: the O-specific polysaccharide, the core polysaccharide, and lipid A.
explanation.whyCorrect: The outermost segment is the O-specific polysaccharide, the O antigen used to identify strains. Inward from it lies the core polysaccharide, and anchoring the molecule into the outer membrane is lipid A. Together these three components constitute the endotoxin of gram-negative organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipoteichoic acid and fimbriae are not components of the LPS molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagellin and capsule are distinct surface structures outside the LPS molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoteichoic acid and mycolic acid belong to gram-positive and mycobacterial walls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptidoglycan and porins are separate cell wall structures, not parts of LPS.

questions.stem: During an outbreak investigation, an E. coli isolate is serotyped and reported as O157:H7. The H portion of this designation refers to an antigen carried on which bacterial structure?

explanation.summary: The H antigen of E. coli is a flagellar antigen; the O antigen is the O-specific polysaccharide of LPS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The O antigen is the O-specific polysaccharide segment of LPS and varies from strain to strain. The H antigen is found in the flagella and is likewise strain specific. Reporting both, as in O157:H7, allows investigators to identify the exact strain responsible for an outbreak.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsule carries the K antigen, such as the K1 capsule of neonatal meningitis strains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The core polysaccharide is an internal segment of LPS and is not used for typing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fimbriae mediate attachment and are not the source of the H designation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Porins are membrane channels and carry neither the O nor the H antigen.

questions.stem: During an outbreak of bloody diarrhea traced to ground beef, a public health laboratory wants a rapid way to separate the suspected enterohemorrhagic strains from other E. coli present in stool. Which biochemical feature is used for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: EHEC are nonmotile, unlike other strains such as ETEC

choices.label: B
choices.text: EHEC are urease positive, unlike other strains such as ETEC

choices.label: C
choices.text: EHEC do not ferment sorbitol, unlike other strains such as ETEC

choices.label: D
choices.text: EHEC ferment lactose slowly, unlike other strains such as ETEC

choices.label: E
choices.text: EHEC produce H2S on TSI, unlike other strains such as ETEC

explanation.summary: EHEC strains fail to ferment sorbitol, while other E. coli strains such as ETEC ferment it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sorbitol fermentation is the practical laboratory handle for separating EHEC from the rest of E. coli. Other strains, including ETEC, ferment sorbitol, whereas EHEC do not. Serotyping for the O157 and H7 antigens then confirms the outbreak strain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is motile, which is the basis of its flagellar H antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is urease negative, which is one of the features that distinguishes it from Proteus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E. coli as a species is a fast lactose fermenter, so this does not separate the strains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E. coli does not produce H2S on TSI agar regardless of strain.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl develops pallor, petechiae, and rising creatinine one week after an episode of bloody diarrhea. Laboratory studies show anemia with fragmented red cells, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure. Which mechanism best explains the anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody against the O157 antigen opsonizes red cells for splenic clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endotoxin activates complement directly on the red cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red cells are sheared by microthrombi on damaged glomerular endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism invades the marrow and suppresses erythrocyte production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxin inserts pores directly into circulating red blood cell membranes

explanation.summary: In HUS, toxin-damaged glomerular endothelium seeds microthrombi that mechanically shear red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shiga-like toxin circulates and binds the glomerular endothelium, causing injury that induces platelet aggregation at the site. The resulting microthrombi create protrusions in the vessels that shear red cells and platelets flowing through the kidney. That damage produces the HUS triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HUS is not an antibody-mediated immune hemolysis directed at the O antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement-mediated lysis on red cells is not the mechanism described for HUS here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow invasion is not part of the pathogenesis of this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The toxin damages endothelium and inhibits protein synthesis rather than lysing red cells directly.

questions.stem: A toxin elaborated by an enterohemorrhagic strain of E. coli is studied in cultured enterocytes. The toxin halts translation in the exposed cells. Which action accounts for this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cleaves the 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit and blocks initiation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depolymerizes actin filaments and effaces the surface microvilli

choices.label: C
choices.text: It forms membrane pores that cause osmotic lysis of the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inactivates the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: It raises intracellular cAMP, driving secretion of water and electrolytes

explanation.summary: Shiga-like toxin inhibits the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit and stops protein synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shiga-like toxin is sufficient on its own to produce necrosis and inflammation in the gut. It also inhibits the 28S rRNA on the 60S large ribosomal subunit, thereby blocking protein synthesis in enterocytes. The same toxin circulates to the kidney and binds glomerular endothelium, causing renal damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The toxin acts on the large subunit, not the 16S rRNA of the small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microvillus effacement occurs by actin condensation at the attachment site, not by this toxin's catalytic action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shiga-like toxin is not a pore-forming toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising cAMP is the action of the heat-labile enterotoxin of ETEC, not Shiga-like toxin.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man develops profuse watery, nonbloody diarrhea on the fourth day of a trip abroad. He is afebrile, and stool studies show no leukocytes. The responsible organism attaches to the brush border of the small intestine with fimbriae and secretes enterotoxins without entering the epithelial cells. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Traveler's diarrhea from a noninvasive, enterotoxin-secreting strain attached by fimbriae is ETEC.
explanation.whyCorrect: ETEC uses fimbriae to attach to the brush border of the small intestine and then releases heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins. Because it does not invade intestinal cells, the illness is a noninflammatory watery diarrhea without fecal leukocytes. This is the classic traveler's diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EHEC causes dysentery and hemorrhagic colitis and can be complicated by HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EIEC invades the large intestine and produces fever with bloody, inflammatory diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EPEC uses adherence factors and effaces microvilli rather than secreting enterotoxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UPEC causes urinary tract infection, not gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: The two enterotoxins released by enterotoxigenic E. coli alter enzyme cascades in intestinal cells, causing hypermotility and efflux of water and electrolytes. Which pairing of toxin and second messenger is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both toxins raise cAMP, with no effect on cGMP levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both toxins raise cGMP, with no effect on cAMP levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heat-labile toxin raises calcium; heat-stable toxin raises cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heat-labile toxin raises cAMP; heat-stable toxin raises cGMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heat-labile toxin raises cGMP; heat-stable toxin raises cAMP

explanation.summary: ETEC heat-labile toxin is the cAMP-inducing toxin and heat-stable toxin is the cGMP-inducing toxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: After attaching to the brush border, ETEC releases both a heat-labile toxin that raises cyclic AMP and a heat-stable toxin that raises cyclic GMP. The rise in both second messengers increases small intestinal motility and drives water and electrolytes into the lumen. The result is the watery, noninflammatory diarrhea of ETEC infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The heat-stable toxin acts through cGMP, so cGMP does rise.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heat-labile toxin acts through cAMP, so cAMP does rise.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither ETEC toxin is described as acting through intracellular calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The assignments are reversed; heat-labile is the cAMP toxin.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant in a developing country has several days of watery, nonbloody stools without fever. Small bowel biopsy shows flattened microvilli with pedestals of polymerized actin beneath adherent bacteria, and no organisms are seen within the enterocytes. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Actin pedestals with effaced microvilli and watery diarrhea in an infant point to EPEC.
explanation.whyCorrect: EPEC attaches to the brush border with adherence factors and uses enzymes to efface, or flatten, the microvilli, forming actin pedestals. The deformed lining absorbs water and nutrients poorly, and the resulting osmotic imbalance produces watery diarrhea. EPEC is noninvasive and is seen especially in infants in developing countries.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EHEC causes bloody diarrhea and releases Shiga-like toxin, neither of which is present here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EIEC invades colonic cells and causes fever with bloody, inflammatory diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ETEC works through secreted heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins, not actin pedestals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UPEC is a urinary tract pathogen and does not cause this intestinal picture.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has fever, cramping, and bloody diarrhea with abundant fecal leukocytes. Stool culture grows an E. coli strain whose clinical presentation is nearly indistinguishable from Shigella infection. Which mechanism best describes how this strain causes disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ascends the mucosa using P pili and forms a protective surface biofilm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attaches to the brush border and secretes cAMP- and cGMP-raising enterotoxins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Effaces microvilli with actin pedestals without entering the epithelial cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forces endocytosis, lyses the phagosome, and replicates with lateral spread

choices.label: E
choices.text: Releases a toxin that inactivates the 60S subunit of glomerular endothelium

explanation.summary: EIEC invades large intestinal cells, escapes the phagosome, and spreads laterally to cause dysentery.
explanation.whyCorrect: EIEC contains enzymes that force host cells of the large intestine to endocytose the bacteria. Once inside, the organisms lyse the phagosome and replicate in the cytoplasm, then spread laterally and destroy the cells. The resulting necrosis and inflammation produce dysentery, which closely resembles Shigella infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: P pili and biofilm are UPEC features used to ascend the urinary tract.
whyWrongByChoice.B: That is ETEC, which is noninvasive and causes watery, noninflammatory diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That is EPEC, which is noninvasive and causes watery diarrhea in infants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That describes the Shiga-like toxin of EHEC acting in HUS, not invasion.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools three days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a family cookout. One week later he becomes pale and oliguric, with a falling platelet count and a rising creatinine. Which organism is most likely responsible?
