explanation.summary: Bloody diarrhea after undercooked beef followed by HUS is enterohemorrhagic E. coli, typically O157:H7.
explanation.whyCorrect: EHEC causes dysentery and hemorrhagic colitis and is the strain associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome. Its Shiga-like toxin circulates and binds glomerular endothelium, producing the triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. Outbreaks of the O157:H7 strain are classically traced to contaminated ground beef.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EIEC causes dysentery but is not the strain associated with HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EPEC causes noninflammatory watery diarrhea, chiefly in infants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ETEC causes watery traveler's diarrhea without blood and does not cause HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UPEC is a urinary pathogen and does not produce bloody diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency, and her urinalysis shows nitrites and leukocytes. The E. coli recovered from her urine ascended from the periurethral area into the bladder. Which bacterial structure allowed the organism to attach to and climb the urinary tract?

explanation.summary: Uropathogenic E. coli attach to and ascend the urinary tract using fimbriae, specifically P pili.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fimbriae are short surface appendages that let E. coli attach to and move along surfaces such as the urothelium. UPEC uses a specialized fimbria called P pili for this purpose, and also forms a biofilm and elaborates hemolysin as it advances. Progressive ascent can carry the infection from cystitis to pyelonephritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binary fission increases the bacterial population but is not a mechanism of attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cilia occur in some microbes but are not found on E. coli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation transfers genetic material and does not mediate adherence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterotoxins alter cell metabolism and enzymes but do not confer attachment or motility.

questions.stem: Uropathogenic E. coli recovered from a patient with recurrent cystitis are shown to form a dense matrix-encased layer on the bladder epithelium. What advantage does this structure confer on the organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows the organism to ferment lactose more rapidly

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inactivates the ribosomes of the uroepithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neutralizes urinary acid so the organism can survive

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shields the organism from immune recognition and eradication

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies the flagellar power needed to reach the kidney

explanation.summary: UPEC form a biofilm that helps them evade immunologic recognition and eradication.
explanation.whyCorrect: After attaching with P pili, UPEC create a biofilm on the urinary tract surface. The biofilm allows the organisms to evade immunologic recognition and clearance, which contributes to persistent and recurrent infection. Hemolysin then helps them invade tissue as they ascend toward the kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactose fermentation is a metabolic property unrelated to biofilm formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of host ribosomes is the action of Shiga-like toxin in EHEC disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urea hydrolysis and alkalinization are features of urease-positive organisms such as Proteus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Motility comes from flagella, not from the biofilm matrix.

questions.stem: A specimen heavily contaminated with gram-positive flora is submitted for recovery of an enteric gram-negative rod. The technologist plates it on eosin methylene blue agar. Which property of this medium makes it suitable for the task?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its dyes inhibit the growth of gram-positive bacteria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its ferrous sulfate precipitates any organism that produces hydrogen sulfide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its high salt concentration inhibits growth of gram-negative bacteria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its phenol red indicator turns yellow only for gram-positive organisms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its sheep blood component lyses only the beta-hemolytic organisms

explanation.summary: EMB agar is selective for gram-negative organisms because its two dyes suppress gram-positive growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: EMB contains eosin and methylene blue, which inhibit the growth of gram-positive bacteria while allowing gram-negative organisms to grow. It is also differential: lactose fermenters stain black, and E. coli forms colonies with a green metallic sheen. MacConkey agar serves the analogous selective and differential role using lactose and a pH indicator.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrous sulfate is a component of TSI agar, where it reveals H2S production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EMB selects against gram-positives, and it is not a high-salt medium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenol red is the pH indicator in TSI agar and reports sugar fermentation, not Gram status.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis is read on blood agar, which is a different medium entirely.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 24-year-old woman presents to an outpatient clinic with two days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has had no recent hospitalization, instrumentation, or antibiotics. Which organism is the single most common cause of her infection?

explanation.summary: E. coli is by far the most common cause of community-acquired urinary tract infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: E. coli accounts for roughly 80 percent of urinary tract infections acquired in the community. Uropathogenic strains use P pili to attach, biofilm to evade the immune system, and hemolysin to invade tissue. The other enteric organisms account for much smaller shares outside the hospital.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida is an uncommon community-acquired cause and appears mainly in hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterococcus falls among the other gram-positive causes, which are far less frequent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella becomes more prevalent in nosocomial rather than community-acquired UTI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proteus causes a minority of urinary infections and is more prominent in the hospital setting.

questions.stem: An infection control review compares urinary isolates from clinic patients with those from patients who developed catheter-associated infection after several weeks in the hospital. E. coli remains the leading isolate in both settings, but a group of other Enterobacteriaceae accounts for a much larger share in the hospital group. Which organisms are these?

explanation.summary: In nosocomial UTI, E. coli still leads but Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Serratia become far more prevalent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Comorbidities and immunosuppression in hospitalized patients give these opportunists the chance they need to cause urinary infection. Antibiotic resistance is also extremely common among nosocomial isolates, which complicates therapy. E. coli nonetheless remains the most common single cause of UTI in both settings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These comma-shaped gram-negative rods cause gastrointestinal disease, not nosocomial UTI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These gram-negative organisms are respiratory and mucosal pathogens, not enteric urinary opportunists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These enteric organisms cause gastrointestinal illness rather than catheter-associated UTI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are gram-positive organisms and are not members of the Enterobacteriaceae.

questions.stem: A 6-day-old neonate is brought in with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, and a bulging fontanelle. Cerebrospinal fluid shows numerous neutrophils, and Gram stain reveals gram-negative rods. Which organism is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli expressing the K1 capsule

explanation.summary: E. coli, especially K1 capsule strains, is the most common gram-negative cause of neonatal meningitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among newborns, E. coli is the leading gram-negative cause of meningitis, and the strains responsible characteristically express the K1 capsule. Penetration of the blood-brain barrier is driven by high-level bacteremia together with virulence factors that interact with receptors on the brain vasculature. Group B Streptococcus and Listeria are the other common neonatal causes but are gram-positive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H. influenzae type b is a pathogen of older infants and children, not of the first week of life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Listeria is a gram-positive rod, which does not match the Gram stain described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N. meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus and is not a typical newborn pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Group B Streptococcus is a gram-positive coccus despite being a common neonatal cause.

questions.stem: The capsule expressed by the E. coli strains that cause neonatal meningitis provokes a strikingly poor host antibody response. Which explanation best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks the O antigen from binding complement and prevents cell lysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is composed of lipid A, which the immune system cannot recognize

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is degraded by host urease before an antibody response can develop

choices.label: D
choices.text: It mimics glycopeptides of the human CNS, so the host is tolerized to it

choices.label: E
choices.text: It varies so rapidly between strains that no antibody can be produced

explanation.summary: The K1 capsule resembles host CNS glycopeptides, so the immune system is tolerized to it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The K1 capsule is structurally identical to the capsule of Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B, and both resemble brain glycopeptides of the central nervous system. Because of that similarity to self, humans are tolerized to the capsule and mount a poor response against it. The organism then reaches the meninges through high-grade bacteremia and factors that engage receptors on brain vasculature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsule's role is molecular mimicry rather than shielding the O antigen from complement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipid A is part of LPS, not of the polysaccharide capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. coli is urease negative, and capsule degradation is not the mechanism of immune evasion here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antigenic variation of the capsule is not the explanation taught for K1 strains.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis. Besides E. coli, which two organisms should be considered the most likely causes at this age?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Group B Streptococcus and Listeria monocytogenes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae type b and enteroviruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neisseria meningitidis and herpes simplex virus

explanation.summary: In newborns, the common causes of meningitis are Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Newborns from birth to about six months are most often infected by Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. S. agalactiae and L. monocytogenes are therefore the expected companions to E. coli in this age group. The pathogen list shifts to S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and H. influenzae type b in older children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryptococcus is associated with HIV infection, not with neonatal meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. influenzae type b and enteroviruses belong to the 6-month to 6-year age band.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N. meningitidis and HSV are causes in older children and adults, not newborns.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These organisms dominate in children and adults rather than in the first months of life.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis is started on empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin. The clinical picture raises concern for Listeria as a possible cause. Which agent should be added to the regimen?

explanation.summary: Ampicillin is added to empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin when Listeria is suspected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Standard empiric coverage for bacterial meningitis is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Neither agent reliably covers Listeria monocytogenes, so ampicillin is added whenever Listeria is a consideration, such as in newborns and older adults. Coverage is then narrowed once the organism is identified.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Azithromycin does not provide the coverage needed for this pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gentamicin is not the agent specified for adding Listeria coverage in this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and is not used for Listeria meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rifampin is used in other settings and is not added for Listeria coverage.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoes laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid diverticulum with gross spillage of colonic contents into the peritoneum. Which statement best characterizes the infection that is expected to follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mixed infection with aerobic and anaerobic bowel flora, including E. coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single-organism infection with Shigella derived from the colonic mucosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: A toxin-mediated illness caused by Shiga-like toxin released into the peritoneum

choices.label: D
choices.text: A viral peritonitis acquired from previously contaminated drinking water

choices.label: E
choices.text: An infection limited to gram-positive skin flora introduced during surgery

explanation.summary: Bowel perforation seeds the peritoneum with mixed flora, and E. coli from the GI tract is a central player.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intraabdominal infections occur when the bowel is perforated and E. coli from the GI tract contaminates the abdominal cavity. These are typically mixed infections containing both aerobic and anaerobic organisms. The number and variety of organisms depend on the severity of the bowel damage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Shigella is an ingested pathogen causing dysentery, not normal colonic flora spilled at perforation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shiga-like toxin is an EHEC product that acts on enterocytes and glomerular endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perforation-related peritonitis is a bacterial process, not a waterborne viral one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Contamination comes from the bowel lumen, so enteric flora rather than skin flora predominate.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with pyelonephritis has a temperature of 39.1 C, blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 28/min, new confusion, and an elevated serum lactate. Which term best describes her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute diarrhea, watery stools lasting fewer than 14 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cystitis, a bladder infection without systemic findings

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysentery, an inflammatory diarrhea with fever and blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemolytic uremic syndrome, with anemia and kidney failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sepsis, a source of infection plus vital sign instability

explanation.summary: Sepsis is a severe systemic inflammatory response defined by a source of infection plus vital sign instability.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sepsis requires a source of infection together with instabilities such as fever, hypotension, and tachypnea, along with indices such as altered mental status and lactic acidosis. This patient has a urinary source plus all of those findings. Sepsis may arise on its own or as a consequence of a primary infection spreading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute diarrhea describes loose stools of less than 14 days' duration, which she does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cystitis is confined to the bladder and lacks the systemic instability seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysentery is a diarrheal syndrome and does not describe this systemic presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HUS is a triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure after EHEC infection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 900/mm3. On hospital day 5 she develops fever and a productive cough, and sputum culture grows E. coli. Which statement best characterizes this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fecal-orally transmitted infection acquired from contaminated food

choices.label: B
choices.text: A toxin-mediated illness from Shiga-like toxin acting in the airway

choices.label: C
choices.text: An opportunistic health care-associated infection favored by neutropenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of a latent E. coli infection residing in the alveoli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traveler's diarrhea presenting atypically in the respiratory tract

explanation.summary: Beyond virulence factors, opportunity determines infection risk, and neutropenic inpatients acquire health care-associated E. coli infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pathogenicity in this family depends on virulence factors, but opportunity matters just as much. A patient undergoing chemotherapy with a low white blood cell count can readily contract a health care-associated infection such as E. coli pneumonia after contamination by visitors or hospital personnel. Immunocompromised hosts are specifically susceptible to these infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fecal-oral spread produces gastroenteritis, not a hospital-acquired pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Shiga-like toxin is an EHEC virulence factor of intestinal and renal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E. coli does not establish latency in the alveoli and reactivate later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Traveler's diarrhea is an ETEC intestinal illness and does not occur in the lung.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought in after three days of sudden-onset loose, watery stools. He is alert but fussy. Which element of the physical examination is most important in assessing the danger posed by his illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assessment of volume status for signs of dehydration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Auscultation of the lungs for focal consolidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Examination of the joints for effusion and warmth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inspection of the skin for a petechial rash

choices.label: E
choices.text: Palpation of the liver for hepatic enlargement

explanation.summary: Acute diarrhea is dangerous mainly because of rapid dehydration, so volume assessment drives management.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute diarrhea is a sudden onset of loose or watery stools lasting less than 14 days, and its principal danger is rapid volume loss. The examination should target vital signs for tachycardia and low blood pressure or orthostatic drops, plus dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, reduced urine output, cool extremities, and a sunken fontanelle in infants. Most cases do not require antibiotics as long as hydration can be maintained.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pulmonary findings do not address the dehydration that makes acute diarrhea dangerous.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Joint examination does not evaluate the volume loss that drives risk in this illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A petechial rash points toward other diagnoses and is not the focus of this assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver size is not the element that determines safe management of acute diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever to 103.6°F (39.8°C), productive cough, worsening shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. She is a college student who binge drinks heavily and consumed more than seven drinks at a party the previous weekend. Her sputum is thick, sticky, and reddish. A chest radiograph shows dense consolidation of the right upper lobe. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-negative bacilli, and culture grows mucoid, lactose-fermenting, indole-negative colonies. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Thick, sticky "red currant jelly" sputum in a patient with alcohol use disorder, together with mucoid lactose-fermenting indole-negative colonies, identifies Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: K. pneumoniae is part of the normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and causes pneumonia most often in hospitalized patients and in people with alcohol use disorder, because aspiration of oral and gastrointestinal contents is common after heavy drinking. Its large mucoid polysaccharide capsule makes the sputum thick, sticky, and reddish, the classic "red currant jelly sputum." In the laboratory it is a gram-negative rod that ferments lactose rapidly but does not produce indole, and its colonies are visibly mucoid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli also ferments lactose rapidly, but it is indole positive and its colonies are not mucoid, and it does not produce currant jelly sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose and causes urinary tract infections far more often than pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia ferments lactose only slowly and is a minor cause of respiratory infection, usually in immunocompromised hosts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus, which does not fit the gram-negative bacilli seen on this patient's sputum Gram stain.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old hospitalized man with alcohol use disorder has lobar pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. His expectorated sputum is thick, sticky, and reddish, which the attending physician describes to the team as "red currant jelly" sputum. Which of the following bacterial structures is most directly responsible for this sputum appearance?

explanation.summary: The currant jelly appearance of Klebsiella sputum comes from the organism's large mucoid polysaccharide capsule.
explanation.whyCorrect: K. pneumoniae produces an unusually large mucoid polysaccharide capsule. Shed into the airway secretions, this capsular material gives the sputum a thick, sticky, slimy consistency, which combined with blood gives the reddish currant jelly appearance. The same capsule makes colonies on agar look slimy, as though someone blew their nose on the plate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-lactamase is a secreted antibiotic-inactivating enzyme and plays no part in the appearance of sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is the endotoxin that drives fever and the septic response; it does not change sputum consistency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: K. pneumoniae is nonmotile, so flagella are not a feature of this organism at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fimbriae mediate adherence to host epithelium and have no effect on the viscosity of secretions.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in the intensive care unit has been mechanically ventilated for 8 days when he develops fever, purulent secretions, and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Endotracheal aspirate grows a gram-negative bacillus that is also a normal inhabitant of his gastrointestinal tract. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, particularly in ventilated patients, and it comes from the patient's own gut flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Members of the Enterobacteriaceae, especially E. coli and K. pneumoniae, are among the most common causes of hospital-acquired infection, and K. pneumoniae is a leading cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Because it colonizes the gastrointestinal tract normally, a hospitalized patient can be infected by his own flora as well as by contaminated equipment or staff hands. Sepsis may follow as a complication of the pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspergillus is a mold, not a gram-negative bacillus, and is not a gastrointestinal commensal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B. pertussis is a coccobacillus causing whooping cough in the community, not ventilator-associated pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Legionella is a ventilator-associated pathogen but is acquired from contaminated water systems, not from the patient's gut flora.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall and cannot be seen as a gram-negative bacillus on Gram stain.

questions.stem: Two gram-negative bacilli isolated from separate hospitalized patients both ferment lactose rapidly on MacConkey agar. Tryptophan-containing broth is inoculated with each isolate and a color-change reagent is added: isolate 1 develops a red layer at the surface, while isolate 2 remains yellow. Isolate 1 is most likely which of the following?

explanation.summary: The indole test separates the two rapid lactose fermenters: E. coli makes indole from tryptophan and K. pneumoniae does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: The indole test detects whether an organism can produce indole from tryptophan; a color-change reagent turns red when indole is present. E. coli is indole positive, so isolate 1 is E. coli. This is one of the standard ways to tell E. coli from K. pneumoniae, since both are gram-negative rods that ferment lactose quickly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter ferments lactose rapidly but is indole negative, which is exactly what distinguishes it from E. coli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K. pneumoniae does not produce indole from tryptophan, so it would give the yellow result seen with isolate 2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. mirabilis is indole negative and also does not ferment lactose, so it fails both parts of the description.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia ferments lactose only slowly, so it does not match the rapid fermentation described in the stem.

questions.stem: A laboratory technologist stabs semi-solid motility agar with five different Enterobacteriaceae isolates. Four of them produce diffuse, hazy growth spreading well away from the stab line; one grows only along the line of inoculation. The isolate that grew only along the stab line is most likely which of the following?

explanation.summary: Among the common Enterobacteriaceae, Klebsiella is the nonmotile one; growth confined to the stab line means no motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strains of Klebsiella are usually nonmotile, so they cannot spread away from the point of inoculation in semi-solid agar and growth stays along the stab line. This is a useful additional way to separate K. pneumoniae from E. coli, which is motile, and it is one of the features listed for Klebsiella alongside its mucoid capsule and indole-negative reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter species are motile and would also produce diffuse growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is motile and would produce the diffuse growth away from the stab line.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. mirabilis is the most motile organism in this group and swarms vigorously across agar surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia species are motile and would spread through semi-solid agar.

questions.stem: A MacConkey agar plate inoculated with a tracheal aspirate from a hospitalized patient grows pink colonies that are strikingly slimy and string out when touched with an inoculating loop. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Pink (lactose-fermenting) colonies that are distinctly mucoid and slimy on MacConkey agar are characteristic of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both E. coli and K. pneumoniae have a capsule, but the Klebsiella capsule is mucoid, so its colonies look very slimy in culture. Combined with pink color from lactose fermentation, this mucoid colony appearance is a practical way to pick K. pneumoniae out from other lactose fermenters at the bench.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli ferments lactose and turns pink on MacConkey agar, but its colonies are not mucoid or stringy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose, so its colonies remain colorless on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudomonas does not ferment lactose and would not produce pink colonies on this medium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella does not ferment lactose and forms colorless, non-mucoid colonies.

questions.stem: A blood isolate of Klebsiella pneumoniae from a hospitalized patient is resistant to ampicillin and to ceftriaxone, and the laboratory reports the strain as an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producer. Which of the following best describes the activity of the responsible enzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acetylates chloramphenicol so the drug can no longer bind ribosomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It methylates the 30S ribosomal subunit so aminoglycosides cannot bind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It pumps fluoroquinolone molecules out of the bacterial cytoplasm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It substitutes an altered penicillin-binding protein into the cell wall.

explanation.summary: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases are enzymes that break down commonly used beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rates of resistance to penicillin and cephalosporin among the Enterobacteriaceae have risen substantially over the last decade, and strains carrying these enzymes are collectively called ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae. The enzymes destroy the beta-lactam ring, rendering penicillins and cephalosporins ineffective, so providers must fall back on intravenous carbapenems for infections that used to be treated with oral agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylation of chloramphenicol is a separate enzymatic resistance mechanism unrelated to beta-lactam drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ribosomal methylation is an aminoglycoside resistance mechanism and would not confer resistance to penicillins or cephalosporins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Efflux pumps expel drugs such as fluoroquinolones; they are not what the term beta-lactamase describes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An altered penicillin-binding protein is the basis of methicillin resistance in staphylococci, not of ESBL production.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with no chronic medical problems, no recent hospitalization, and no indwelling devices is found to have a urinary tract infection caused by an ESBL-producing Escherichia coli. A medical student is surprised that a healthy outpatient could acquire such an organism. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About one in four patients with an ESBL infection has no known underlying health condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: ESBL infections arise only after a patient completes a prolonged course of carbapenems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ESBL production is restricted to Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter rather than Enterobacteriaceae.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae have steadily declined in the United States since 2012.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ESBL-producing organisms are essentially confined to ICU patients with indwelling devices.

explanation.summary: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are a concern in the community as well as in health care, and roughly a quarter of infected patients have no known underlying illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: What is particularly problematic about ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae is that they infect otherwise healthy patients at an alarming rate: about one out of four patients with an ESBL infection has no known underlying health condition. These organisms spread rapidly and can cause or complicate infections in healthy people as well as in health care settings, which is why they carry a serious threat rating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbapenem exposure selects for carbapenem resistance; ESBL infections occur without any such prior therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ESBL is by definition a property of Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli and K. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cases of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae have increased since 2012, not declined.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ESBL-producing organisms are a documented concern in the community, not just among device-associated ICU patients.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old hospitalized man has bacteremia caused by an ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Susceptibility testing shows resistance to ceftriaxone, cefepime, ampicillin, and piperacillin. Which of the following intravenous agents is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation.summary: ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae can still be treated with carbapenems, which is why providers must often switch from oral agents to intravenous carbapenem therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotic options for ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are limited because the enzyme destroys penicillins and cephalosporins. Health care providers therefore often have to use intravenous carbapenem antibiotics, such as meropenem, to treat infections that would previously have been managed with oral drugs. The downside is that heavier carbapenem use is itself driving the rise of carbapenem-resistant strains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral penicillin combination and is not adequate for an ESBL bloodstream infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ampicillin-sulbactam is a penicillin combination and falls within the spectrum of drugs the enzyme destroys.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cefoxitin is a cephalosporin and therefore shares the same vulnerability to the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ceftazidime is a cephalosporin and is inactivated by the extended-spectrum beta-lactamase.

questions.stem: An infection-control team is reviewing carbapenem resistance among Enterobacteriaceae isolates at their hospital. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance develops only in strains that do not also produce ESBL enzymes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance has been essentially eliminated from United States hospitals since 2012.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance is confined to community-acquired rather than nosocomial isolates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbapenem resistance is far more common in Escherichia coli than in Klebsiella pneumoniae.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Roughly 11% of nosocomial Klebsiella pneumoniae infections are carbapenem resistant.

explanation.summary: Although both E. coli and K. pneumoniae can be carbapenem resistant, resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae, about 11% of nosocomial isolates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased use of carbapenems to treat ESBL infections has driven a rise in carbapenem resistance. Both E. coli and K. pneumoniae can be carbapenem resistant, but resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae, with roughly 11% of all nosocomial K. pneumoniae infections carbapenem resistant. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae carry an urgent threat rating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ESBL production and carbapenem resistance frequently coexist; in fact carbapenem use to treat ESBL strains selects for the latter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbapenem resistance remains a major concern in United States health care facilities and has not been eliminated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae are principally a problem of health care facilities, not the community.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The relationship is the reverse: carbapenem resistance is much more common in K. pneumoniae than in E. coli.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old hospitalized woman with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and a central venous catheter develops bacteremia with a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) isolate. Her family asks about her prognosis. Mortality from CRE infection in hospitalized patients with comorbidities has been reported to be as high as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Mortality from carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection has been reported as high as 50% in hospitalized patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae are resistant to nearly all available antibiotics, leaving only more toxic or less effective treatment options. Mortality can be extremely high, especially in hospitalized patients with comorbidities, and has been reported as high as 50% in hospitalized patients who contract CRE infections. This severity is why CRE is designated an urgent threat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1% mortality figure greatly underestimates the lethality of CRE infection in comorbid hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 5% mortality figure is far below the reported rate for CRE infections in this population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 15% mortality figure still substantially understates the reported CRE mortality in hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 90% mortality figure overstates the reported rate; even in the sickest hospitalized patients it reaches about 50%.

questions.stem: On one hospital ward, unrelated isolates of Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae are all found to carry the same carbapenemase gene. Which of the following best explains how this resistance gene moved among these different species?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spontaneous chromosomal point mutation arose independently within each species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each species sporulated and passed the gene along within a resistant spore coat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene integrated into human host DNA and was later returned to the bacteria.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gene was carried on a plasmid and transferred between cells by conjugation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gene was displayed on the bacterial capsule and swapped during cell clumping.

explanation.summary: Antibiotic resistance genes in the Enterobacteriaceae are usually carried on plasmids that move between bacteria by conjugation.
explanation.whyCorrect: These antibiotic resistance genes are usually encoded on a plasmid that transfers between bacteria via conjugation, which is why the identical gene can appear in several different genera on the same ward. Other forms of horizontal transfer may also contribute to the spread. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae in particular carry mobile genetic elements that are easily shared between bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Independent identical point mutations in three separate species is vanishingly unlikely and would not produce one shared gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterobacteriaceae are not spore formers, so spore-mediated transfer is not possible for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bacterial resistance genes are not routed through human genomic DNA on their way between bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is a protective polysaccharide layer and is not a vehicle for exchanging genes.

questions.stem: A hospital epidemiologist is identifying which patients are at highest risk of acquiring a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection. Which of the following patients is at greatest risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healthy toddler in daycare with an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hospitalized patient with an indwelling urinary catheter on a long antibiotic course

choices.label: C
choices.text: A marathon runner using an inhaled bronchodilator for exercise-induced asthma

choices.label: D
choices.text: A teenager taking oral antihistamines for seasonal allergic rhinitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: An outpatient finishing a 5-day course of oral penicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis

explanation.summary: Patients who require devices such as catheters and those taking long courses of antibiotics are at greatest risk for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: CRE is a problem of health care facilities. Patients who require indwelling devices such as urinary catheters and patients taking long courses of certain antibiotics are the ones most at risk for CRE infections. Both factors are present in this patient: an invasive device gives the organism access past normal barriers, and prolonged antibiotic exposure selects for resistant flora.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A healthy child with a self-limited viral illness has neither device exposure nor prolonged antibiotic pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An inhaled bronchodilator involves no invasive device and no antibiotic selection pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihistamines for allergic rhinitis do not create antibiotic pressure or breach any barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A brief outpatient antibiotic course without hospitalization or devices confers little CRE risk.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with lobar pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which of the following best explains why his heavy drinking predisposed him to this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol directly dissolves alveolar surfactant and collapses the dependent lung.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol induces capsule production by Klebsiella strains colonizing the airway.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol intoxication promotes aspiration of oral and gastrointestinal flora into the lungs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alcohol raises gastric pH and allows Klebsiella to colonize the gastric mucosa.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alcohol suppresses bone marrow granulopoiesis and produces profound neutropenia.

explanation.summary: People with alcohol use disorder get Klebsiella pneumonia because heavy drinking makes aspiration of normal oral and gut flora into the lung far more likely.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aspiration of foreign material such as food, liquid, saliva, or vomit is more common after heavy drinking. This floods the lungs with the normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and the oral cavity, and K. pneumoniae is a normal gut inhabitant. Once seeded into the lung it can cause a severe, sometimes necrotizing pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Surfactant destruction is not the described mechanism linking alcohol use to Klebsiella pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The capsule is a constitutive feature of the organism and is not induced by the host's alcohol intake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella reaches the lung by aspiration of existing flora, not by newly colonizing the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The predisposition is explained by aspiration of flora rather than by an alcohol-induced neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is brought in after an episode of heavy drinking followed by repeated vomiting. Two weeks later he has a cough productive of foul-smelling sputum. Culture grows several different anaerobic organisms with differing antibiotic susceptibilities, making therapy difficult. Which of the following groups of organisms is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Aspiration of oral cavity flora produces a mixed anaerobic pneumonia with foul-smelling sputum, caused by organisms such as Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, and Prevotella.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infections caused by normal flora of the oral cavity are mixed infections of anaerobic bacteria, specifically Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, and Prevotella species. Because several different bacteria are involved and each may have different antibiotic resistance, treatment is difficult. Pneumonias caused by oral anaerobes classically produce foul-smelling sputum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These are facultative gram-negative rods from the lower gut; aspirated gut flora does not give the foul-smelling anaerobic picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither organism is an oral anaerobe, and neither accounts for the mixed anaerobic growth described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These Enterobacteriaceae cause infections in the immunocompromised and hospitalized, not mixed anaerobic aspiration pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are typical community-acquired pneumonia organisms and are not anaerobes of the oral cavity.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with epilepsy has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Three days later he develops fever and a productive cough, and a chest radiograph shows a right-sided infiltrate. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his increased risk of pneumonia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspiration of oropharyngeal and gastric contents during the convulsion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct inoculation of the airway by contaminated respiratory equipment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding of the lung from an occult urinary tract infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Person-to-person droplet transmission from a household contact

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of a latent granuloma in the apex of the right upper lobe

explanation.summary: Patients who have seizures are at risk for Klebsiella and other pneumonias because of aspiration during the event.
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of airway protection during a seizure allows oral and gastric contents to be aspirated into the lung, carrying normal flora of the oral cavity and gastrointestinal tract with them. This is the same mechanism that puts patients with alcohol use disorder at risk, and it is why patients with seizures are also susceptible to K. pneumoniae lung infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: He was at home and not intubated, so contaminated respiratory equipment plays no role here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no evidence of a urinary source, and this patient's risk relates to the seizure itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Droplet spread from a contact does not explain the specific temporal link to the seizure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivation of a latent granuloma describes tuberculosis, not a post-seizure bacterial pneumonia.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with severe lobar pneumonia has serial chest radiographs. The initial film shows dense consolidation; a film obtained one week later shows a lucent cavity within the consolidated lobe as lung tissue is destroyed. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause a necrotizing pneumonia that destroys lung tissue and leaves a cavity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In severe cases K. pneumoniae causes a necrotizing pneumonia, which leads to cavitation. As the infection progresses, a cavity appears within the area of consolidation because lung tissue has been destroyed. This progression is characteristic and is one reason K. pneumoniae pneumonia is so feared in hospitalized patients and those with alcohol use disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter causes pneumonia mainly in immunocompromised hospitalized patients and is not known for cavitation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycoplasma causes a mild atypical pneumonia without tissue destruction or cavity formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia is only a minor cause of respiratory infection and is not associated with this necrotizing picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes lobar consolidation with rusty sputum but is not the organism described as producing cavitation here.

questions.stem: Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a range of infections in hospitalized and immunocompromised patients. Which of the following is the least common of its manifestations, occurring typically in the immunocompromised host?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nosocomial pneumonia in a ventilated patient

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary tract infection in a hospitalized patient with bladder disease

explanation.summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an uncommon cause of meningitis, and when it does cause it, the patient is typically immunocompromised.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the infections K. pneumoniae causes, meningitis stands out as the uncommon one and is typically seen in immunocompromised patients. Pneumonia, urinary tract infection, septicemia, and wound or surgical site infections are all well-recognized and considerably more frequent presentations in hospitalized patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumonia is very common with this organism, particularly in the hospital and in ventilated patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Septicemia is a well-recognized complication of Klebsiella pneumonia and can also occur on its own.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wound and surgical site infections are among the routinely listed infections caused by K. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary tract infection is uncommon in the community but its risk is clearly increased in hospitalized patients with bladder disease.

questions.stem: An infection-control nurse is teaching new staff about how Klebsiella pneumoniae spreads on a surgical ward. Which of the following best describes how patients typically acquire this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bite from an arthropod vector that circulates in warm climates

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ingestion of undercooked poultry contaminated during processing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhalation of spores aerosolized from hospital soil and potted plants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Person-to-person contact, contaminated equipment, or the patient's own flora

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sexual contact with a partner colonized in the genital tract

explanation.summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae spreads by person-to-person contact, contaminated surfaces and equipment, or infection with the patient's own normal flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transmission of K. pneumoniae occurs through person-to-person contact, contaminated surfaces or medical equipment, and infection with the patient's own normal flora. Because the organism already lives in the gastrointestinal tract of healthy people, a hospitalized patient does not need an external source to become infected, which is part of why it is such a persistent hospital adversary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no arthropod vector for Klebsiella transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foodborne ingestion is not the route by which Klebsiella infections are acquired in the hospital.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is not a spore former, and environmental spore inhalation describes fungal pathogens instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Klebsiella is not transmitted as a sexually acquired infection.

questions.stem: A critical care team classifies the organisms that cause ventilator-associated pneumonia as either multidrug-resistant (MDR) or non-MDR pathogens in order to guide empiric therapy. Which of the following is classified as an MDR pathogen?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa heads the list of multidrug-resistant causes of ventilator-associated pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microbiologic causes of ventilator-associated pneumonia are divided into non-MDR pathogens and MDR pathogens. The MDR group includes Pseudomonas aeruginosa, methicillin-resistant S. aureus, Acinetobacter species, antibiotic-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL-positive and carbapenem-resistant strains), Legionella pneumophila, Burkholderia cepacia, and Aspergillus species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotic-sensitive Enterobacteriaceae, including E. coli, are non-MDR; only the resistant strains are MDR.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. influenzae is listed among the non-MDR pathogens causing ventilator-associated pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methicillin-sensitive S. aureus is a non-MDR pathogen; it is MRSA that falls in the MDR group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is the first organism listed in the non-MDR column.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has dysuria and suprapubic pain. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 8.5, well above her usual slightly acidic range, and culture grows a gram-negative bacillus that swarms across the agar plate. Production of which of the following enzymes best explains the alkaline urine?

explanation.summary: Proteus mirabilis produces urease, which splits urea into ammonia and raises the pH of the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urine is normally neutral or slightly acidic. During a urinary tract infection, P. mirabilis causes the pH of the urine to rise because it produces urease, which cleaves urea to form carbon dioxide and ammonia. Urinary tract infection is by far the most common disease caused by P. mirabilis, and the swarming motility described in the stem is its signature laboratory feature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide and has no effect on the pH of urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulase is a virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus and does not alter urinary pH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaluronidase degrades connective tissue ground substance and does not generate ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lecithinase damages cell membranes and plays no role in alkalinizing the urine.

questions.stem: Proteus mirabilis raises urinary pH during infection by cleaving urea with the enzyme urease. Which of the following pairs of products is generated by this reaction?

explanation.summary: Urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, and the ammonia is what alkalinizes the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reaction is urea plus water, acted on by urease, yielding two molecules of ammonia and one of carbon dioxide. The ammonia raises urinary pH, which allows calcium-containing compounds to precipitate and allows ammonia to combine into ammonium magnesium phosphate. That is the chain of events linking urease-producing organisms to stone formation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose and lactate are products of carbohydrate metabolism, not of urea hydrolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrogen sulfide is produced on TSI agar by organisms such as Proteus, but it is not a product of urease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrite production reflects nitrate reduction by urinary bacteria, a separate reaction from urea splitting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uric acid is a purine breakdown product and is not generated by urease.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with recurrent Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infections passes a stone. Stone analysis confirms that it formed in alkaline urine from the ammonia generated by bacterial splitting of urea. This stone is most likely composed of which of the following?

explanation.summary: Ammonia generated by bacterial urease combines into ammonium magnesium phosphate, known as struvite.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides raising urinary pH, the ammonia released by urease can form a compound called ammonium magnesium phosphate, or struvite. Struvite stones account for about 15% of kidney and bladder stones and can grow to enormous size, sometimes requiring surgery for removal. They are the stones specifically associated with urease-producing urinary pathogens such as P. mirabilis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common urinary stones overall but are not the ones formed from bacterial ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystine stones result from an inherited defect in amino acid transport, not from bacterial urea splitting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uric acid stones form in acidic urine, the opposite of the alkaline urine produced by urease activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Xanthine stones arise from a disorder of purine metabolism and have no relationship to urease.

questions.stem: A urologist reviews an abdominal radiograph from a patient with chronic Proteus mirabilis urinary infection and sees a large, branching, radiodense stone filling the renal collecting system. Which of the following statements about this type of stone is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are radiolucent and can be identified only by contrast-enhanced ultrasonography.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They form in acidic urine produced by organisms that consume rather than make ammonia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They make up about 15% of urinary stones and are called staghorn calculi.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They make up about 70% of urinary stones and almost always remain very small.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They reliably dissolve with hydration alone and therefore never require surgical removal.

explanation.summary: Struvite stones account for about 15% of kidney and bladder stones and can branch into the deer-antler shape called a staghorn calculus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Struvite stones account for 15% of kidney and bladder stones and can get very large. In some instances the stone grows so big that surgery must be used to remove it. As they enlarge they branch and come to resemble the horns of a deer, which is why they are called staghorn calculi, and they are visible on plain radiographs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These stones are radiodense and are classically identified on a plain abdominal radiograph.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Struvite stones form specifically in alkaline urine created by urease-producing organisms that generate ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Struvite accounts for about 15% of stones, not 70%, and these stones are notable for becoming very large.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Large staghorn calculi frequently require surgical removal rather than resolving with hydration.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine pH is 5.5, and the gram-negative bacillus grown from her urine tests urease negative. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: E. coli strains typically do not produce urease, which distinguishes E. coli from the other common urinary pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many bacteria that cause urinary tract infections produce urease, including K. pneumoniae, S. saprophyticus, U. urealyticum, P. aeruginosa, and S. epidermidis. E. coli strains typically do not produce urease, so a urease-negative gram-negative urinary isolate with an acidic urine pH points to E. coli, and these patients do not develop struvite stones from their infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: K. pneumoniae is urease positive and so does not fit a urease-negative isolate in acidic urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. mirabilis is a strong urease producer and would raise the urine pH rather than leave it at 5.5.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus produces urease, and it is a gram-positive coccus rather than a gram-negative bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: U. urealyticum is named for its urease activity and would not give a urease-negative result.

questions.stem: Both Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are gram-negative bacilli that ferment lactose rapidly and cause hospital-acquired infections. Which of the following findings would be expected with E. coli but not with K. pneumoniae?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A green metallic sheen when grown on eosin methylene blue agar

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacillary morphology on Gram stain of sputum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth of pink colonies on MacConkey agar within 24 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presence of a polysaccharide capsule surrounding the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ability to cause hospital-acquired pneumonia and septicemia

explanation.summary: Although both organisms ferment lactose, only E. coli produces the green metallic sheen on eosin methylene blue agar.
explanation.whyCorrect: E. coli and K. pneumoniae look the same in several respects: both are gram-negative bacilli, both are fast lactose fermenters, and both have a capsule. Among their listed key features, the green metallic sheen on EMB agar belongs to E. coli alone, along with indole positivity and beta-hemolysis. Colony appearance is the other practical discriminator, since the Klebsiella capsule makes its colonies mucoid and slimy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Both are gram-negative bacilli, so Gram stain morphology is identical for the two organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both organisms ferment lactose rapidly and produce pink colonies on MacConkey agar, so this does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both E. coli and K. pneumoniae have a capsule; the difference is that the Klebsiella capsule is mucoid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both are among the most common causes of hospital-acquired infection, including pneumonia and septicemia.

questions.stem: A microbiology student seeds the center of a semi-solid agar plate with a gram-negative bacillus isolated from urine. Over the next day the growth advances outward from the inoculation point in a series of concentric rings, forming a bull's-eye pattern across the plate. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Proteus mirabilis is exceptionally motile, and its swarming motility produces the concentric bull's-eye colonies on agar.
explanation.whyCorrect: A distinguishing characteristic of P. mirabilis is its mobility; it is incredibly motile and its motility is described as swarming. Most motile bacteria will not move far from where they were seeded on a semi-solid agar because such agar is hard to move through, but as P. mirabilis colonies grow they move across the agar and form bull's eyes. This same motility helps the organism ascend the urinary tract.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter is motile but is not the organism known for swarming bull's-eye colony formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is motile but will not spread across semi-solid agar in concentric swarming rings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K. pneumoniae is nonmotile and would remain confined to the point of inoculation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia is motile but does not display the swarming bull's-eye growth characteristic of Proteus.

questions.stem: A gram-negative bacillus isolated from the urine of a hospitalized man produces colorless colonies on MacConkey agar and blackens the butt of a triple sugar iron (TSI) slant. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Proteus mirabilis does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide on TSI agar, a combination that separates it from the other Enterobacteriaceae.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. mirabilis is a gram-negative bacillus that does not ferment lactose, so colonies stay colorless on MacConkey agar. It also produces hydrogen sulfide on TSI agar, which blackens the medium. Taken together these traits distinguish P. mirabilis from the other gram-negative bacilli, and in the identification algorithm the non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-negative, hydrogen sulfide-producing group is Salmonella and Proteus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter ferments lactose rapidly and so would produce pink colonies on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli ferments lactose rapidly and produces pink colonies with a surrounding halo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K. pneumoniae ferments lactose rapidly, so its colonies would be pink rather than colorless.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia ferments lactose, albeit slowly, and is not the organism characterized by hydrogen sulfide production here.

questions.stem: A nosocomial isolate from an intensive care patient is a motile, urease-positive, gram-negative bacillus that does not ferment lactose. The laboratory must determine whether the organism is Proteus mirabilis or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following tests best distinguishes the two?

explanation.summary: Proteus mirabilis is oxidase negative and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is oxidase positive, so the oxidase test separates these two non-lactose fermenters.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. mirabilis is oxidase negative, which distinguishes it from P. aeruginosa, another cause of nosocomial infections. In the gram-negative bacillus identification algorithm, non-lactose fermenters are split by the oxidase test: oxidase-positive isolates are Pseudomonas, while oxidase-negative isolates go on to hydrogen sulfide testing to separate Shigella and Yersinia from Salmonella and Proteus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both are gram-negative bacilli, so their Gram stain appearance is the same.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither organism ferments lactose, so both give colorless colonies on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both organisms are motile, so a motility test cannot tell them apart.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both P. mirabilis and P. aeruginosa are urease producers that can contribute to urinary stone formation.

questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with bloody diarrhea is a gram-negative bacillus that does not ferment lactose, is oxidase negative, and produces no hydrogen sulfide on triple sugar iron agar. Which of the following pairs of genera best fits this profile?

explanation.summary: In the gram-negative identification algorithm, non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-negative bacilli that do not make hydrogen sulfide are Shigella and Yersinia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The algorithm works down from gram-negative bacilli through lactose fermentation. Non-fermenters are separated by oxidase: oxidase-positive isolates are Pseudomonas, and oxidase-negative isolates are then tested for hydrogen sulfide production on TSI agar. Those that do not produce hydrogen sulfide are Shigella and Yersinia; those that do are Salmonella and Proteus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter and Serratia are slow lactose fermenters rather than non-fermenters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Escherichia and Klebsiella are fast lactose fermenters and so drop out at the first branch point.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudomonas and Burkholderia are oxidase positive, which excludes them from this branch.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella and Proteus are the hydrogen sulfide-positive branch, so they do not fit a negative TSI result.

questions.stem: A wound culture from an immunocompromised hospitalized patient grows a gram-negative bacillus that ferments lactose slowly and forms strikingly bright red colonies on the agar plate. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Red pigment production together with slow lactose fermentation identifies Serratia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some, but not all, species of Serratia produce a red pigment called prodigiosin, and Serratia species are slow lactose fermenters, so colonies on MacConkey or EMB agar do not change color as quickly as those of fast fermenters. The pigment is also useful outside the clinical laboratory, since it reveals when a biofilm, such as the pink film on bathroom tile, contains the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterobacter ferments lactose rapidly and does not make a red pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli ferments lactose rapidly and produces no red pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K. pneumoniae forms mucoid, non-pigmented colonies and ferments lactose rapidly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. mirabilis does not ferment lactose and does not produce a red pigment.

questions.stem: Colonies of a gram-negative bacillus on a MacConkey plate are colorless at 24 hours. At 48 hours they have turned pink, but no pink halo surrounds them, unlike the Escherichia coli colonies growing on the same plate. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism cannot ferment lactose at all under any condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism ferments lactose slowly rather than rapidly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism has lost its outer membrane and stains unpredictably.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism produces hydrogen sulfide, which darkens the medium.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produces urease, which alkalinizes the surrounding agar.

explanation.summary: Citrobacter and Serratia are slow lactose fermenters, so their colonies take 48 hours or longer to turn pink and lack the halo seen with fast fermenters.
explanation.whyCorrect: It typically takes 48 hours or more before colonies of Citrobacter turn pink on MacConkey agar, and they usually do not have the pink halo around the colony that is typically seen with fast lactose-fermenting bacteria. Serratia behaves the same way. Because they ferment lactose slowly, Serratia and Citrobacter can be distinguished from E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and Enterobacter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A true non-fermenter such as Proteus would still be colorless at 48 hours, but these colonies did turn pink.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the outer membrane is not a real phenomenon here and would not explain delayed pink colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrogen sulfide production blackens TSI agar and is not what delays the color change on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urease activity is not what governs the timing of the lactose-driven color change on this medium.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient develops a bloodstream infection with an Enterobacter species, and the isolate proves resistant to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics. Which of the following best explains why drug resistance is such a common problem with this genus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most strains produce beta-lactamase, which inactivates beta-lactam drugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are obligate intracellular organisms shielded from antibiotic exposure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They form endospores that survive standard hospital disinfection procedures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They grow only as biofilms that physically exclude all classes of antibiotic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack a peptidoglycan cell wall, so beta-lactam drugs have no target.

explanation.summary: Drug resistance is a substantial problem with Enterobacter because most strains produce beta-lactamase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterobacter species are part of the normal gastrointestinal flora and cause urinary tract infections, septicemia, lower respiratory tract infections, and wound infections in the immunocompromised. Drug resistance is a substantial problem with this genus because most strains produce beta-lactamase, an enzyme that destroys beta-lactam antibiotics and narrows the therapeutic options.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterobacter are not obligate intracellular organisms; they grow readily on routine laboratory media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterobacter species are not spore formers, so spore survival is not the resistance mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterobacter grow as free-living organisms as well, and biofilm formation is not the stated cause of their resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enterobacter are gram-negative bacteria with a peptidoglycan cell wall, so beta-lactams do have a target.

questions.stem: A gram-negative bacillus isolated from the urine of an immunocompromised patient ferments lactose rapidly, is motile, is indole negative, and is weakly urease positive. Its colonies are somewhat mucoid but noticeably less slimy than those of Klebsiella. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: A motile, fast lactose-fermenting, indole-negative, weakly urease-positive rod with partially mucoid colonies is Enterobacter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like all Enterobacteriaceae, Enterobacter species are gram-negative rods, and they ferment lactose rapidly like E. coli and K. pneumoniae. However, Enterobacter are indole negative, which distinguishes them from E. coli, and they are motile and only weakly urease positive. While some strains of Enterobacter can produce mucoid colonies, they are not as slimy as those of Klebsiella.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrobacter is a slow lactose fermenter, which conflicts with the rapid fermentation described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E. coli is indole positive and urease negative, which contradicts two of the results given.
whyWrongByChoice.D: K. pneumoniae is nonmotile and forms distinctly mucoid, slimy colonies rather than partially mucoid ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serratia ferments lactose slowly and is urease negative, so it does not fit this biochemical profile.

questions.stem: A laboratory is working to separate a slow lactose-fermenting, nonpigmented gram-negative bacillus from Escherichia coli. The genus in question takes its name from a metabolic capability that it possesses. Which of the following statements best describes that capability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts citrate into hydrogen sulfide, blackening the butt of a TSI slant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reduces nitrate to nitrite far more rapidly than Escherichia coli does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It releases a citrus-scented volatile compound detectable in broth culture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires a citrate-buffered medium before it can ferment lactose at all.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses citrate as a carbon source, which Escherichia coli typically cannot.

explanation.summary: Citrobacter gets its name from its ability to use citrate as a carbon source, which E. coli typically cannot do.
explanation.whyCorrect: Citrobacter is named for its capacity to use citrate as its carbon source. This can further assist in distinguishing it from E. coli, which typically cannot use citrate as an energy source. The test is only an assist and not definitive, because other members of the Enterobacteriaceae can also use citrate as an energy source. Pigment production by Serratia is the other feature used to separate these two slow lactose fermenters, although not all Serratia species make pigment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrogen sulfide production on TSI agar is a separate trait and is not related to citrate utilization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitrate reduction is a shared property of Enterobacteriaceae and is not the source of the genus name.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The name refers to citrate utilization as a nutrient, not to any aromatic compound produced in culture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Citrate is used as a carbon source; it is not a requirement for the organism to ferment lactose.

questions.stem: Serratia, Citrobacter, and Enterobacter species are normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and are widely distributed in soil, water, and food. Which of the following patients is most likely to develop an invasive infection with one of these organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healthy adult taking oral antihistamines for seasonal allergic rhinitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A healthy college athlete two days after competing in an indoor swim meet

choices.label: C
choices.text: A healthy traveler using a scopolamine patch for motion sickness at sea

choices.label: D
choices.text: A hospitalized immunocompromised patient with an indwelling urinary catheter

choices.label: E
choices.text: A well-appearing toddler in daycare with a self-limited viral exanthem

explanation.summary: Serratia, Citrobacter, and Enterobacter typically cause infection only in immunocompromised or hospitalized patients, especially those with invasive devices.
explanation.whyCorrect: These three genera live harmlessly in the gastrointestinal tract of healthy people and typically only cause infections in the immunocompromised or in hospitalized patients. Most Citrobacter infections in particular occur in hospitals and other health care facilities, and the patients who contract them are usually immunocompromised, have invasive devices such as a catheter, or both. Their infections include urinary tract, respiratory tract, wound, eye, and bloodstream infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamine use for allergic rhinitis does not cause immunosuppression or breach a barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A healthy athlete has neither the immunocompromise nor the invasive device that these organisms require.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A transdermal motion sickness patch is not an invasive device and creates no risk for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A well toddler with a viral rash is immunologically intact and has no portal for invasive infection.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has 4 days of progressive weakness in both legs, preceded by numbness and tingling in her feet. The tingling has now started in her hands. Two weeks ago she had several days of abdominal cramping and diarrhea that was watery at first and later dark; it resolved without treatment. Cerebrospinal fluid shows elevated protein with a normal cell count. Which of the following organisms most likely preceded her current illness?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter spp. are the most common cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: An ascending sensory and motor neuropathy beginning 1-3 weeks after a diarrheal illness, with elevated CSF protein and a normal cell count, is Guillain-Barre syndrome. About 1 in every 1,000 people with a Campylobacter infection develops GBS, and Campylobacter spp. are the leading cause in the U.S. The mechanism is molecular mimicry: bacterial proteins resemble proteins in the nervous system, so the immune response against the bacteria also attacks nerves.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli makes Shiga toxin and is associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome, not with a demyelinating neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Typhoid fever presents with prolonged fever, headache, hepatosplenomegaly, and a transient truncal rash, and is not the organism linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella causes bacillary dysentery with small-volume bloody stools and tenesmus; its neurologic sequel is not Guillain-Barre syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is associated with day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis, not with Guillain-Barre syndrome.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has fever and bloody diarrhea that started 2 days after a barbecue. A stool isolate is a gram-negative straight rod that forms colorless colonies on MacConkey agar and is oxidase negative. On triple sugar iron agar the butt is yellow and a black precipitate is present. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: A black precipitate on TSI agar means H2S production, which separates Salmonella from Shigella.
explanation.whyCorrect: Salmonella spp. are gram-negative rods that do not ferment lactose and are oxidase negative. They ferment glucose, which acidifies and yellows the TSI butt, and they produce H2S, which forms the black precipitate. That combination identifies Salmonella in this isolate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter spp. are oxidase positive and are comma- or S-shaped rather than straight rods.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan that causes amebic dysentery and liver abscess and is not grown on these bacterial agars.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Escherichia coli ferments lactose, so it would form colored colonies on MacConkey agar rather than colorless ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella spp. are also non-lactose fermenting and oxidase negative, but they do not produce H2S, so there is no black precipitate on TSI agar.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl develops fever and bloody diarrhea. Within a week, three of her four household members become ill with the same illness despite no shared meals, and the family reports only casual hand contact. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with illness after ingesting only 10 to 100 organisms?

explanation.summary: Shigella spp. have an extremely low infectious dose, estimated at 10-100 organisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shigella spp. have adapted to the acidic environment of the stomach, so very few organisms survive to reach the colon and cause disease. This very low infectious dose explains easy person-to-person spread by hands and contaminated surfaces, and it is why even flies can transfer the bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter spp. are usually acquired from contaminated poultry, raw milk, or water rather than from a 10-100 organism inoculum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan cause of dysentery and liver abscess, not a low-dose bacterial pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Typhoidal Salmonella is spread by contaminated food and water from human carriers and is not characterized by this very low dose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nontyphoidal Salmonella generally requires a large ingested dose because it is not well adapted to stomach acid.
