questions.stem: A 26-year-old man planning travel to South Asia receives an inactivated vaccine made from a purified capsular polysaccharide. He asks whether it will also protect him from the Salmonella gastroenteritis he read about in a recent poultry outbreak at home. Which of the following best explains why it will not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nontyphoidal serotypes are not members of the family Enterobacteriaceae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nontyphoidal serotypes are restricted to human and primate reservoirs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nontyphoidal serotypes do not express the O antigen of lipopolysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nontyphoidal serotypes do not possess the Vi antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nontyphoidal serotypes lack flagella and therefore lack the H antigen

explanation.summary: Typhoid vaccines target the Vi capsular antigen, which nontyphoidal Salmonella do not have.
explanation.whyCorrect: One distinction of the Salmonella subtypes that cause typhoid fever is a capsule composed of the polysaccharide Vi antigen. Inactivated typhoid vaccines use purified Vi antigen to protect travelers going to regions where typhoidal salmonellosis is prevalent. Because nontyphoidal Salmonella spp. do not have the Vi antigen, these vaccines are not effective against them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both typhoidal and nontyphoidal Salmonella are members of Enterobacteriaceae, so family membership does not explain the gap in coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is the typhoid-causing serotypes that are restricted to humans; nontyphoidal serotypes have wide animal reservoirs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The O antigen of lipopolysaccharide is one of the three key antigens used to serotype Salmonella and is present across the genus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nontyphoidal Salmonella are motile and use flagellar H antigen in serotyping, so they are not missing flagella.

questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with watery diarrhea after drinking raw milk is a gram-negative curved rod. The laboratory reports that the organism failed to grow well on the standard 37 degrees C plate but grew abundantly when incubated at 42 degrees C. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with this finding?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter spp. grow optimally at 42 degrees C, unlike most human pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most bacteria that infect humans grow best at 37 degrees C, but Campylobacter spp. grow optimally at 42 degrees C. Selective incubation at that temperature is a standard way to recover the organism from stool, and it pairs with the comma or S shape seen on Gram stain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli invades colonic mucosa but is a straight rod with no elevated growth temperature requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Salmonella enterica serotype Enteritidis is a straight rod that grows on MacConkey and EMB agar at standard incubation temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella dysenteriae is a straight gram-negative rod recovered on routine enteric media incubated at 37 degrees C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is linked to day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis and is not identified by growth at 42 degrees C.

questions.stem: Three gram-negative enteric isolates from patients with bloody diarrhea are tested. Two are oxidase negative; the third is oxidase positive. Which of the following conclusions about the oxidase-positive isolate is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a lactose fermenter rather than a non-lactose fermenter

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a Shiga toxin producer rather than a non-producer

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is Campylobacter rather than Salmonella or Shigella

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is Salmonella rather than Shigella or Campylobacter

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is Shigella rather than Salmonella or Campylobacter

explanation.summary: Oxidase production separates Campylobacter from Salmonella and Shigella.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter spp. produce oxidase, while Salmonella spp. and Shigella spp. are oxidase negative. Oxidase therefore sorts the bloody-diarrhea isolates into Campylobacter versus the two enteric genera, and it complements the morphologic clue that Campylobacter is comma- or S-shaped while the others are straight rods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxidase testing measures a respiratory enzyme and says nothing about whether the organism ferments lactose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Shiga toxin production is a property of S. dysenteriae type I and EHEC and is unrelated to the oxidase reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella spp. are oxidase negative and catalase positive, so a positive oxidase test argues against Salmonella.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella spp. are oxidase negative, so a positive test argues against Shigella.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, decreased urine output, and bruising. Laboratory studies show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a rising creatinine. The responsible toxin is an AB toxin whose enzymatically active A component enters host cells. Which of the following best describes the action of that component?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks the release of the neurotransmitters GABA and glycine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creates double-stranded breaks in host cell DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Crosslinks T-cell receptors to MHC class II molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inactivates the 60S subunit of the ribosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increases intracellular cyclic AMP by ADP-ribosylation

explanation.summary: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit and halts protein synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shigella dysenteriae type I and enterohemorrhagic E. coli both produce Shiga toxin, an AB toxin in which the B subunit binds the target cell and the A subunit acts inside it. The A subunit inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit, blocking protein synthesis and killing the cell. When the toxin leaks out of the GI tract it destroys red cells and injures the kidney, producing hemolytic uremic syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking release of GABA and glycine is the mechanism of tetanospasmin, the tetanus toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Causing double-stranded DNA breaks is the mechanism of cytolethal distending toxin of Campylobacter spp.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crosslinking the T-cell receptor to MHC class II is how superantigens such as TSST-1 and SpeA act.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising cyclic AMP by ADP-ribosylation is the mechanism of heat-labile toxin of E. coli and several other bacterial toxins.

questions.stem: An intestinal biopsy from a patient with bacillary dysentery shows bacteria inside colonic epithelial cells, many with a comet-like tail of host cytoskeletal filaments extending from one end and some already within neighboring cells. The isolate has no flagella. Which of the following best explains how this organism reaches adjacent cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is carried between cells inside migrating tissue macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: It polymerizes host actin at one pole and is propelled forward

choices.label: C
choices.text: It re-enters the lumen and is taken up again by distant M cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes a toxin that opens epithelial tight junctions

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses a polar flagellum to swim through the mucus layer

explanation.summary: Shigella spp. are non-motile but spread cell to cell using host actin polymerization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike Salmonella spp., Shigella spp. are non-motile and have neither flagella nor cilia. They express proteins that cause host actin to polymerize at one end of the bacterium, producing a rocket-like effect that shoots the organism out of its current cell and into flanking cells. This is how the infection spreads laterally through the epithelium after initial entry through M cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Shigella kills the macrophages it encounters and spreads directly between epithelial cells rather than riding inside them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spread is direct from one cell into flanking cells, not by a second round of luminal uptake at distant M cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella injures epithelium through invasion, inflammation, and apoptosis rather than by a toxin that opens tight junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A polar flagellum is a feature of Campylobacter spp.; Shigella spp. have no flagella at all.

questions.stem: After ingestion, Salmonella spp. reach the small intestine and first invade a specialized epithelial cell that normally samples luminal antigens and hands them to immune cells. Which of the following cells does the organism exploit for this initial entry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterochromaffin cells of the gastric antrum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Goblet cells of the colonic crypts

choices.label: C
choices.text: M cells overlying the Peyer patches

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paneth cells at the base of the crypts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parietal cells of the gastric fundus

explanation.summary: Salmonella spp. enter through M cells of the Peyer patches to reach gut tissue and lymph nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: M cells are specialized epithelial cells found in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, particularly the Peyer patches of the small intestine, and their normal job is to transport antigens from the lumen to immune cells. Salmonella spp. use them to gain access to the tissue of the GI tract and local lymph nodes. Once through, the organism infects neutrophils, macrophages, and dendritic cells as a facultative intracellular pathogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterochromaffin cells are hormone-secreting cells and are not the portal of entry described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Goblet cells secrete mucus and are not the antigen-sampling route the organism exploits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paneth cells release antimicrobial peptides into the crypt lumen rather than transporting antigen across the epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parietal cells secrete gastric acid, which Salmonella tolerates poorly; they are not an entry route.

questions.stem: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp. all use a needle-like apparatus that spans the inner and outer membranes of the bacterium. Which of the following best describes what this structure accomplishes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It anchors lipopolysaccharide to the outer leaflet of the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: It exports a capsular polysaccharide that blocks complement deposition

choices.label: C
choices.text: It injects effector proteins that drive bacterial entry into host cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It pumps antibiotics out of the bacterial cytoplasm into the environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transfers plasmid DNA between adjacent bacteria during conjugation

explanation.summary: The type III secretion system injects effector proteins that force host cells to take the bacterium in.
explanation.whyCorrect: The type III secretion system is a needle-like structure that injects host cells with effector proteins. Those effectors facilitate entry of the bacteria into cells and prevent destruction of the bacteria once they have been phagocytized, and the infected cells are eventually destroyed. All three genera in this brick use a T3SS for this purpose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipopolysaccharide is a structural component of the outer membrane and is not positioned by this apparatus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capsule export is a separate process; the Vi capsule of typhoidal Salmonella is not delivered by the secretion needle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotic efflux is performed by membrane pumps and is unrelated to the injection apparatus described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasmid transfer during conjugation uses a sex pilus, not the effector-injecting needle.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia has 5 days of fever and worsening right thigh pain after an episode of diarrhea. Imaging shows osteomyelitis of the femur, and blood cultures grow a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to this disseminated infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent terminal complement components of the membrane attack complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective neutrophil oxidative burst from an NADPH oxidase defect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Functional asplenia from repeated splenic infarction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired mucosal IgA secretion across the intestinal epithelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of gastric acid from long-term acid suppression therapy

explanation.summary: Sickle cell anemia causes autosplenectomy, and asplenic patients are prone to disseminated salmonellosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Invasive Salmonella disease is rare but occurs in children, patients over 50, the immunocompromised, and patients without spleens or with poorly functioning spleens. In sickle cell anemia, abnormally shaped red blood cells drive repeated splenic infarcts, progressively destroying the spleen. This autosplenectomy leaves the patient susceptible to disseminated salmonellosis, which can present as septicemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, or meningitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Terminal complement deficiency is not the explanation offered for disseminated Salmonella in sickle cell anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective neutrophil oxidative burst is not the mechanism described for salmonellosis risk in sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucosal IgA secretion is not the defect that makes these patients prone to invasive Salmonella infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced gastric acid lowers the dose needed for infection but does not account for bone and bloodstream dissemination here.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has 2 weeks of knee and ankle pain, red eyes, and burning with urination. Three weeks earlier he had a self-limited episode of bloody diarrhea. Which of the following best characterizes his current condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A crystal-induced synovitis precipitated by the preceding illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: A demyelinating process triggered by antibody molecular mimicry

choices.label: C
choices.text: A septic joint seeded by bacteria still present in the synovium

choices.label: D
choices.text: A toxin-mediated arthropathy caused by circulating Shiga toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: An autoimmune arthritis strongly associated with the HLA-B27 allele

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune disease after GI or GU infection, and 70-90% of patients carry HLA-B27.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive arthritis occurs 1-4 weeks after gastrointestinal and genitourinary infections, and its three most common features are conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, remembered as cannot see, pee, or climb a tree. It is unclear exactly why it happens, but 70-90% of patients carry the HLA-B27 allele of MHC class I. Most cases resolve in a few months with anti-inflammatory therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystal-induced synovitis is a separate entity and is not the postinfectious syndrome described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A demyelinating process from molecular mimicry describes Guillain-Barre syndrome, which causes weakness, not arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive arthritis is immune-mediated and follows the infection; it is not a joint with ongoing bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shiga toxin causes hemolytic uremic syndrome, not the conjunctivitis-urethritis-arthritis triad.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman returns from a 3-week trip to South Asia with 10 days of fever, headache, malaise, myalgias, and constipation. She has hepatosplenomegaly, and a transient blanching maculopapular rash is noted on her trunk. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: A transient truncal maculopapular rash with systemic illness points to typhoidal salmonellosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typhoidal Salmonella causes constipation and/or diarrhea along with fever, headache, malaise, chills, myalgias, and vomiting, and it spreads beyond the GI tract through the bloodstream, producing sepsis and hepatosplenomegaly. One distinguishing feature is a transient maculopapular rash on the trunk, which does not occur in nontyphoidal salmonellosis. Typhoidal salmonellosis is common in Africa, Asia, and Latin American countries.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni causes watery or bloody diarrhea over 1-7 days and is not associated with this rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteroinvasive E. coli invades colonic mucosa and causes dysentery without the rash and hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotype Enteritidis is a leading cause of gastroenteritis and does not produce the truncal rash or the systemic picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella flexneri causes bacillary dysentery with small-volume bloody stools rather than a systemic febrile illness with a truncal rash.

questions.stem: A public health team investigates repeated typhoid fever cases traced to meals prepared by one asymptomatic food handler who recovered from typhoid fever 3 years ago. Which of the following best explains her role in these outbreaks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She acquired reinfection repeatedly from an animal reservoir

choices.label: B
choices.text: She has relapsing disease from an antibiotic-resistant isolate

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is among the 1 to 5 percent who become chronic carriers

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is colonized with a nontyphoidal serotype that lacks Vi antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: She is shedding organisms transiently during a prolonged incubation

explanation.summary: One to five percent of people who contract typhoidal salmonellosis become chronic carriers and shed for years.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typhoid-causing serotypes are restricted to humans, so people are the reservoir. About 1 to 5 percent of patients who contract typhoidal salmonellosis become chronic carriers, and they can shed the bacteria for years, potentially infecting those around them. Contaminated food and water prepared by such a carrier facilitate the spread of typhoidal salmonellosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Typhoid-causing serotypes are not found in animal reservoirs, so repeated animal-source reinfection is not possible.
whyWrongByChoice.B: She is asymptomatic rather than clinically relapsing, so ongoing active disease does not explain the cluster.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nontyphoidal serotypes cause gastroenteritis, not the typhoid fever cases being investigated here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The incubation period for typhoid fever is 6 to 30 days, far too short to span 3 years of transmission.

questions.stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman with 2 days of fever, cramping, and nonbloody diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken asks for an antibiotic so that she can return to her job at a day care sooner. Stool testing is positive for Salmonella. Which of the following is the best reason to withhold antibiotics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics increase the risk of postinfectious reactive arthritis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotics interfere with stool culture and serotyping results

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibiotics prevent the development of protective serotype immunity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibiotics prolong shedding of the organism after symptoms resolve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antibiotics trigger release of preformed toxin from dying bacteria

explanation.summary: In healthy patients, antibiotics do not shorten salmonellosis and they lengthen the shedding period.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most cases of salmonellosis resolve on their own with supportive care focused on fluid and electrolyte replacement, and in healthy patients antibiotics do not shorten the duration of fever or diarrhea. Patients may shed Salmonella for months after infection, and antibiotics increase the duration of that shedding because they destroy normal flora, so it takes longer for normal flora to push Salmonella out. Antibiotics should be reserved for severe cases and patients at high risk of severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reactive arthritis follows the infection itself; antibiotic therapy is not described as raising that risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interference with laboratory identification is not the reason given for avoiding antibiotics in healthy patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Withholding antibiotics is not recommended in order to allow protective serotype immunity to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Release of preformed toxin is not the stated reason to avoid antibiotics in nontyphoidal salmonellosis.

questions.stem: During an outbreak investigation, no animal or livestock source can be identified, and every case is linked to person-to-person spread or to food handled by an infected person. Which of the following organisms is found only in humans and primates?

explanation.summary: Shigella spp. are the exception among enteric pathogens: they infect only humans and primates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike most Salmonella spp., Shigella spp. only infect humans and primates and are not carried in livestock as normal flora. They are transmitted by the fecal-oral route and can be spread by contaminated food, water, or skin, typically the hands. That human-only reservoir is why outbreaks trace back to infected people rather than to an animal source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter is found in the gastrointestinal microbiota of many animals, including poultry, cattle, swine, dogs, and cats.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli is carried in livestock and is a frequent source of food contamination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nontyphoidal Salmonella has broad animal reservoirs, especially poultry and eggs, and also reptiles and livestock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is associated with day care outbreaks and is not restricted to a human and primate reservoir.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops fever and diarrhea. The family keeps a pet turtle, and the child frequently handles it before meals. Which of the following organisms is most likely to have been transmitted this way?

explanation.summary: Reptiles and amphibians kept as pets shed Salmonella in their feces and have been traced as an outbreak source.
explanation.whyCorrect: Animals and pets may carry Salmonella spp. and transmit them to humans. Reptiles and amphibians kept as pets can carry and shed the bacteria in their feces, and cases have been traced back to pet reptiles. Livestock, cats, and dogs may also carry the bacteria, and food or water contaminated with animal feces spreads the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter is linked to poultry, raw milk, dairy, seafood, produce, and pets such as dogs and cats.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan spread by fecally contaminated food and water, not by reptile contact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Escherichia coli and its variants are associated with livestock and contaminated food rather than with pet reptiles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella spp. infect only humans and primates, so a turtle cannot serve as the reservoir.

questions.stem: A microbiology laboratory reports that more than 20 species exist in a genus of curved gram-negative rods that cause diarrhea, but that one species dominates human disease. Which of the following species accounts for more than 90% of human infections in this genus?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter jejuni causes more than 90% of human Campylobacter infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are more than 20 species of Campylobacter, but C. jejuni causes more than 90% of human infections. In the United States, Campylobacter spp. are the most common cause of bacterial diarrhea, with more than 1.5 million cases each year, and because most infections are self-resolving, campylobacteriosis is underreported.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter coli is one of the other species in the genus and does not account for the great majority of human cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Campylobacter fetus is another member of the genus but is not the dominant cause of human infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salmonella bongori is one of the two medically significant Salmonella species, not a Campylobacter species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella dysenteriae belongs to a different genus and is the Shiga toxin-producing Shigella species.

questions.stem: A state health department reviews roughly 450,000 annual U.S. cases of an illness caused by a non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Which of the following species accounts for the largest share of these cases in the United States?

explanation.summary: Shigella sonnei is the most common Shigella species in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are 4 major species of Shigella: S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. boydii, and S. sonnei. In the U.S., S. sonnei is the most common, and about 450,000 cases of shigellosis occur in the U.S. annually. Shigella spp. are non-motile, non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-negative gram-negative bacilli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi causes typhoid fever and is motile and H2S producing, unlike the organism described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Shigella boydii is one of the four major species and is not the predominant U.S. isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shigella dysenteriae is the species whose type I strains carry Shiga toxin, but it is not the most common U.S. species.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella flexneri is one of the four major species but does not account for most U.S. cases.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl who had bloody diarrhea 6 days ago now has decreased urine output. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL with schistocytes, a platelet count of 38,000/mm3, and a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL. Which of the following organisms most likely caused her diarrheal illness?

explanation.summary: Only Shigella dysenteriae type I among Shigella carries Shiga toxin and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shigella dysenteriae type I possesses Shiga toxin, the same toxin carried by enterohemorrhagic E. coli, so it can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome. HUS presents with the classic triad of acute kidney injury, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. As the toxin leaks out of the GI tract, destruction of red blood cells causes anemia and significant clotting risk, and the debris of dead cells and clotting injures the kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni produces cytolethal distending toxin and is linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome rather than HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serotype Typhimurium causes gastroenteritis and, when invasive, septicemia or osteomyelitis rather than HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shigella sonnei is the most common U.S. species but is not the Shiga toxin-producing type described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is associated with day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis, not with Shiga toxin disease.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has 3 days of fever, cramping right lower quadrant pain, and watery diarrhea 4 days after a chicken dinner. He is taken to the operating room for presumed appendicitis, but the appendix is normal and the terminal ileum and cecum are inflamed. Which of the following organisms best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter can mimic appendicitis by inflaming the ileum and cecum rather than the appendix.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incubation period for Campylobacter is 2-5 days and symptoms typically last 1-7 days, with diarrhea that is commonly watery, abdominal pain, cramping, fever, and fatigue. Some patients report symptoms that mimic appendicitis; this is typically not due to an inflamed appendix but to inflammation of the ileum and cecum, called ileocecitis. Poultry is a classic source of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic dysentery and liver abscess, not an operative picture of normal appendix with ileocecitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli causes bloody diarrhea and is linked to hemolytic uremic syndrome rather than to ileocecitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Typhoid fever presents with prolonged fever, headache, constipation or diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly, not focal ileocecitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella flexneri causes colitis with frequent small-volume bloody stools and tenesmus rather than a right lower quadrant appendicitis mimic.

questions.stem: Two patients are evaluated on the same day. One became ill 12 hours after a buffet that served undercooked eggs; the other became ill 2 days after her toddler returned from a household with diarrheal illness, and she has small-volume bloody stools. Which of the following correctly pairs the organisms with these intervals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Salmonella 1 to 3 days; Shigella 8 to 72 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: Salmonella 2 to 5 days; Shigella 6 to 30 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salmonella 5 to 7 days; Shigella 1 to 10 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Salmonella 6 to 30 days; Shigella 2 to 5 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salmonella 8 to 72 hours; Shigella 1 to 3 days

explanation.summary: Nontyphoidal Salmonella begins 8 to 72 hours after exposure; shigellosis begins 1 to 3 days after ingestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms of Salmonella typically begin 8 to 72 hours after infection, depending on the number of bacteria consumed. Symptoms of shigellosis begin 1 to 3 days after consumption of the bacteria, starting as watery diarrhea that progresses to dysentery with frequent, small-volume stools containing pus, mucus, and blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the two intervals; the 8 to 72 hour window belongs to Salmonella, not Shigella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two to 5 days is the Campylobacter incubation period, and 6 to 30 days applies to typhoid fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Five to 7 days is how long shigellosis lasts, and 1 to 10 days is the incubation period for paratyphoid fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Six to 30 days is the incubation period for typhoid fever, and 2 to 5 days is the interval for Campylobacter.

questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient with dysentery is a gram-negative straight rod that does not ferment lactose, is oxidase negative, produces no black precipitate on triple sugar iron agar, and shows no movement in motility medium. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with this profile?

explanation.summary: Shigella is non-motile and H2S negative, which separates it from Salmonella in the laboratory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like Salmonella spp., Shigella spp. are gram-negative bacilli, non-lactose fermenters, and oxidase negative. Shigella spp. are non-motile, and when grown on TSI agar there is no black precipitate because they do not produce H2S. This distinguishes Shigella from Salmonella spp., which produce H2S on TSI agar and are motile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni is oxidase positive and comma- or S-shaped rather than a straight, oxidase-negative rod.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Escherichia coli ferments lactose, so it would not match the non-lactose-fermenting result described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotype Enteritidis has flagellar motility and produces H2S, so it would be motile with a black precipitate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serotype Typhi is a motile, H2S-producing Salmonella, so both the motility and TSI results are inconsistent.

questions.stem: A curved gram-negative rod isolated from a patient with diarrhea secretes a toxin that causes double-stranded breaks in host cell DNA, arresting the cell cycle and eventually killing the cell. Which of the following toxins is being described?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter spp. produce cytolethal distending toxin, which breaks host DNA and arrests the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter spp. produce a toxin called cytolethal distending toxin. It causes double-stranded DNA breaks, leading to cell cycle arrest and eventually cell death. Campylobacter also uses a T3SS to force GI cells to endocytose it, adhesion proteins to cling to the epithelium, a polar flagellum for motility, and LPS that damages host tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Heat-labile toxin of E. coli raises intracellular cyclic AMP and does not damage host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit and blocks protein synthesis rather than cleaving DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetanospasmin blocks the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic shock syndrome toxin 1 is a superantigen that crosslinks T-cell receptors to MHC class II.

questions.stem: A reference laboratory subtypes a Salmonella isolate from a multistate outbreak. Which of the following sets of antigens is used to distinguish among the more than 2,600 serotypes of this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lipid A antigen, the mycolic acid antigen, and the Vi antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: The M protein, the teichoic acid antigen, and the capsular K antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: The O antigen of lipopolysaccharide, the flagellar H antigen, and the Vi antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: The peptidoglycan antigen, the porin antigen, and the pilus antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Shiga toxin antigen, the H antigen, and the outer membrane F antigen

explanation.summary: Salmonella serotyping rests on three antigens: O of LPS, H of flagella, and the surface Vi antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The medically significant Salmonella species are S. enterica and S. bongori, and they are further distinguished into serotypes by three key antigens: the O antigen of their LPS, the H antigen of their flagella, and the surface Vi antigen. Collectively there are over 2,600 serotypes, and serotype testing of O, H, and the presence of Vi is used to identify them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mycolic acid is a mycobacterial cell wall lipid and has no role in Salmonella serotyping.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M protein and teichoic acid are gram-positive cell wall components and are not used to serotype Salmonella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan, porins, and pili are not the three antigens on which Salmonella serotyping is based.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin belongs to S. dysenteriae type I and EHEC and is not a Salmonella serotyping antigen.

questions.stem: A traveler develops fever 3 weeks after returning from a region where typhoid fever is endemic. His physician notes that the interval is well within the expected window for this infection but would be unusually long for paratyphoid fever. Which of the following pairs of incubation periods is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Typhoid 1 to 10 days; paratyphoid 6 to 30 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Typhoid 1 to 3 days; paratyphoid 6 to 30 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Typhoid 2 to 5 days; paratyphoid 5 to 7 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Typhoid 6 to 30 days; paratyphoid 1 to 10 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: Typhoid 8 to 72 hours; paratyphoid 1 to 3 days

explanation.summary: Typhoid fever incubates 6 to 30 days; paratyphoid fever incubates 1 to 10 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incubation period for typhoid fever is typically 6 to 30 days, and 1 to 10 days for paratyphoid fever. A febrile illness beginning 3 weeks after exposure therefore fits typhoid fever caused by S. enterica serotype Typhi, while it would fall outside the usual window for S. enterica serotype Paratyphi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the two values; the longer 6 to 30 day window belongs to typhoid, not paratyphoid, fever.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One to 3 days is the onset interval for shigellosis, and the paratyphoid figure is also reversed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two to 5 days is the Campylobacter incubation period, and 5 to 7 days is how long shigellosis lasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eight to 72 hours is the onset interval for nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis, not typhoid fever.

questions.stem: A clinician sends a stool sample for a patient with dysentery and requests both organism identification and an antibiotic resistance assay. The laboratory notes that since 2017 an increasing percentage of isolates of this genus have been resistant to both azithromycin and ciprofloxacin. Which of the following organisms is being discussed?

explanation.summary: Drug resistance is a growing problem in Shigella, with rising dual resistance to azithromycin and ciprofloxacin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Over half of U.S. Shigella infections are antibiotic resistant, and since 2017 an increasing percentage of Shigella isolates have been resistant to both azithromycin and ciprofloxacin. For that reason, testing patient stool samples for Shigella spp. is frequently paired with an antibiotic resistance assay.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter resistance is rising with agricultural antibiotic use, but the azithromycin and ciprofloxacin trend since 2017 describes Shigella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteroinvasive E. coli is characterized by invasion of colonic mucosa rather than by this resistance pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Typhoidal Salmonella is prevented with Vi antigen vaccines; this specific dual-resistance trend is not the one described for it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is associated with day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis, not this resistance trend.

questions.stem: Two enteric pathogens are compared. One reliably causes disease after ingestion of only 10 to 100 organisms, while the other generally requires a large ingested dose. Which of the following best explains the difference between them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The low-dose organism is a facultative intracellular pathogen while the other is not

choices.label: B
choices.text: The low-dose organism is adapted to the acidic environment of the stomach

choices.label: C
choices.text: The low-dose organism is motile while the other is non-motile

choices.label: D
choices.text: The low-dose organism possesses a type III secretion system while the other does not

choices.label: E
choices.text: The low-dose organism produces an exotoxin while the other does not

explanation.summary: Shigella survives gastric acid, so very few organisms are needed; Salmonella tolerates acid poorly and needs a large dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shigella spp. can cause illness with extremely low doses, estimated at 10-100 bacteria, because the genus has adapted to the acidic environment of the stomach. In general it requires a large dose of Salmonella spp. to become infected because those bacteria are not particularly adapted to stomach acid. Acid tolerance, not toxin or invasion machinery, is what separates the two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Salmonella spp. are the facultative intracellular pathogens described in this brick, so this does not explain the low dose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shigella spp. are the non-motile organisms and Salmonella spp. are motile, so this reverses the actual finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both organisms use a type III secretion system to enter M cells, so that feature does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin is limited to S. dysenteriae type I, so exotoxin production does not explain the low dose across the genus.

questions.stem: A public health report notes that a single genus accounts for more than 1.5 million U.S. cases per year and is the most common bacterial cause of diarrhea in the United States, with the true number likely higher because most infections resolve on their own. Which of the following organisms is being described?

explanation.summary: Campylobacter spp. are the most common cause of bacterial diarrhea in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the U.S., Campylobacter spp. are the most common cause of bacterial diarrhea, with more than 1.5 million cases occurring every year. Most infections are self-resolving, so campylobacteriosis is underreported. Campylobacter spp. are also the most common cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome in the U.S.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Approximately 1.35 million cases of salmonellosis occur in the U.S. each year, and Salmonella is not named the most common cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 450,000 cases of shigellosis occur in the U.S. annually, well below the figure described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vibrio spp. are not among the organisms given as leading causes of bacterial diarrhea in this discussion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is noted for day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis rather than for leading U.S. case counts.

questions.stem: A stool sample from a patient with fever and diarrhea is plated on MacConkey agar. One streak yields pink colonies and another yields colorless colonies. Which of the following best explains the colorless colonies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism does not ferment lactose, so the medium is not acidified

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism does not produce catalase, so peroxide accumulates

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism is non-motile, so it cannot spread through the agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism produces H2S, which precipitates and bleaches the colony

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produces oxidase, which oxidizes the indicator dye

explanation.summary: Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose fermenters and therefore form colorless colonies on MacConkey agar.
explanation.whyCorrect: Salmonella spp. are gram-negative rods that do not ferment lactose, and Shigella spp. are likewise non-lactose fermenters. MacConkey and EMB agar can be used to grow Salmonella spp., and the lack of lactose fermentation leaves the indicator unchanged, so the colonies stay pale next to a lactose fermenter such as E. coli.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Salmonella spp. are catalase positive, and catalase activity is not what the MacConkey indicator reports.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Motility does not determine colony color on MacConkey agar; motile Salmonella also forms colorless colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H2S production is demonstrated as a black precipitate on TSI agar, not as colorless colonies on MacConkey.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella and Shigella are oxidase negative, and oxidase is not the reaction that colors MacConkey agar.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old man hospitalized with severe shigellosis develops worsening abdominal distention and absent bowel sounds. Abdominal imaging shows marked dilation of the colon. Which of the following is the greatest immediate risk from this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute kidney injury from circulating Shiga toxin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ascending paralysis from autoimmune nerve injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic carriage with shedding of bacteria for years

explanation.summary: Toxic megacolon in shigellosis enlarges the colon and raises the risk of bowel perforation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complications of shigellosis are rare but occur in the elderly, the immunocompromised, and children. Common complications include sepsis, toxic megacolon, and rectal prolapse. Enlargement of the colon in toxic megacolon increases the risk of bowel perforation, which is the immediate danger in a distended, dilated colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemolytic uremic syndrome requires Shiga toxin from S. dysenteriae type I and is a rare, separate complication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ascending paralysis describes Guillain-Barre syndrome, which follows Campylobacter rather than a dilated colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic carriage for years is a feature of typhoidal salmonellosis, and it is not a consequence of colonic dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteomyelitis is a rare complication of disseminated salmonellosis, not of toxic megacolon in shigellosis.

questions.stem: A Gram stain of a stool culture from a patient with fever and diarrhea after drinking unpasteurized milk shows pink organisms with a comma and S shape. Which of the following additional features is most consistent with this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polar flagellum that facilitates spread through the GI tract

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Vi polysaccharide capsule targeted by an inactivated vaccine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Actin-based propulsion from one pole into neighboring cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-motile with no black precipitate on triple sugar iron agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga toxin production capable of causing hemolytic uremic syndrome

explanation.summary: Campylobacter spp. are comma- or S-shaped gram-negative rods with a polar flagellum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter spp. are gram-negative bacilli with a comma or S shape, which distinguishes them from Salmonella and Shigella spp., which are straight rods. They have a polar flagellum that facilitates mobility and spread of the bacteria in the GI tract, and like all gram-negative bacteria they possess LPS, which damages host tissue. Raw milk is a recognized source.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The Vi capsule belongs to the typhoid-causing Salmonella serotypes, not to curved gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Actin-based propulsion between cells is the motility strategy of non-motile Shigella spp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Being non-motile with no H2S on TSI agar describes Shigella spp., which are straight rods.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin is produced by Shigella dysenteriae type I and enterohemorrhagic E. coli, not by Campylobacter.

questions.stem: A district investigating recurrent typhoid fever plans an intervention. Testing of local poultry flocks, cattle, and household pets is proposed. Which of the following best explains why this approach will not identify the source?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism is killed by the acidic environment of animal stomachs

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism loses the Vi antigen when carried by animals

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism survives only briefly outside a living host

choices.label: D
choices.text: The typhoid-causing serotypes are restricted to human hosts

choices.label: E
choices.text: The typhoid-causing serotypes cannot be grown on standard agars

explanation.summary: Typhoidal Salmonella serotypes have no animal reservoir; humans are the source.
explanation.whyCorrect: One distinction between typhoidal and nontyphoidal Salmonella is that the typhoid-causing serotypes are restricted to humans and are not found in animal reservoirs. Spread occurs through contaminated food and water handled by infected people, including the 1 to 5 percent who become chronic carriers. Testing animals therefore cannot find the source of a typhoid cluster.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Animal gastric acid is not the stated barrier; the serotypes simply do not occupy animal reservoirs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Vi antigen defines the typhoidal serotypes and is not something lost during animal carriage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Environmental survival is not the issue; contaminated food and water readily transmit the organism between people.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella grows on MacConkey, EMB, and TSI agar, so culture is not the limiting factor.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, severe abdominal cramps, and a painful, persistent urge to defecate. She passes frequent, small-volume stools containing pus, mucus, and blood. Which of the following organisms most likely explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: Bacillary dysentery with tenesmus and frequent small-volume bloody stools is the classic picture of shigellosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In shigellosis the diarrhea is watery at first but progresses to dysentery. Patients commonly have frequent, small-volume stools with pus, mucus, and blood, and severe abdominal cramps, tenesmus, fever, anorexia, and fatigue are also common complaints. Symptoms typically resolve in healthy individuals within 5-7 days with supportive therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter diarrhea is commonly watery and becomes bloody only in severe cases, without prominent tenesmus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serotype Enteritidis causes gastroenteritis that is clinically indistinct from other causes, typically with larger-volume diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Typhoid fever causes prolonged fever, headache, hepatosplenomegaly, and a truncal rash rather than small-volume bloody stools.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is characterized by day care outbreaks and pseudoappendicitis rather than this dysentery picture.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man returning from extended travel has 3 weeks of intermittent bloody diarrhea, and imaging now reveals a solitary hepatic abscess. Stool cultures for bacterial enteric pathogens are repeatedly negative. Which of the following organisms best accounts for these findings?

explanation.summary: Among causes of bloody diarrhea, Entamoeba histolytica is the protozoan that causes liver abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bloody diarrhea has several classic causes, and Entamoeba histolytica is the protozoan among them, producing amebic dysentery and liver abscess. Because it is not a bacterium, routine bacterial stool cultures are negative, which fits this patient's repeated negative results alongside a hepatic abscess.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni causes diarrhea that may be bloody and is linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome, not hepatic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enteroinvasive E. coli invades colonic mucosa to cause dysentery but does not produce a liver abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serotype Typhimurium causes gastroenteritis and, when invasive, septicemia or osteomyelitis rather than liver abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shigella dysenteriae causes bacillary dysentery and, through Shiga toxin, hemolytic uremic syndrome rather than liver abscess.

questions.stem: A patient hospitalized with Guillain-Barre syndrome asks about causes other than the diarrheal illness he had 2 weeks ago, noting that he received an influenza vaccine last season. Which of the following statements about the relationship between influenza and this syndrome is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza infection and influenza vaccination carry an equal risk of causing the syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza infection causes the syndrome at roughly 10 times the rate of the vaccine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Influenza vaccination causes the syndrome in about 1 in every 1,000 people vaccinated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither influenza infection nor influenza vaccination has been linked to the syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The influenza vaccine is the single most common cause of the syndrome in the United States

explanation.summary: Influenza infection causes Guillain-Barre syndrome at about 10 times the rate of the influenza vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter is not the only cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Two out of three people with GBS have had a GI or respiratory tract infection before symptom onset, and the flu, cytomegalovirus, EBV, Zika virus, and other viruses are known causes. Rarely, vaccines can cause it: the influenza vaccine causes GBS in 1 or 2 patients per million doses, while the influenza virus itself causes GBS at a rate 10 times higher than the vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The risks are not equal; infection with the virus carries a substantially higher risk than vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 1 in 1,000 is the risk after a Campylobacter infection; the vaccine risk is 1 or 2 per million doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both influenza infection and, rarely, influenza vaccination have been linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Campylobacter spp., not the influenza vaccine, are the most common cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome in the U.S.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man develops an itchy rash two days after spending an evening in a poorly maintained hotel hot tub. Examination shows tender red papules and pustules centered on hair follicles over the trunk and thighs, most dense where his swim trunks sat. He is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Folliculitis following immersion in a poorly maintained hot tub is caused by the water-loving Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: A hot tub that is not properly maintained quickly becomes a breeding ground for water-loving bacteria such as Pseudomonas. Prolonged soaking swells the skin and creates microabrasions that let the organism enter soft tissue. The result is tender, sometimes itchy red papules and pustules focused around hair follicles, which occurs in otherwise healthy people and usually resolves on its own.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida albicans causes intertriginous and mucosal yeast infections, not follicular pustules after water immersion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of skin infection generally, but the hot tub exposure points to Pseudomonas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a low-virulence skin commensal and is not the organism linked to hot tub exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes is a common cause of skin infection but does not have the hot tub and whirlpool association.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 12-year-old competitive swimmer has three days of right ear pain and drainage. Pulling on the auricle reproduces the pain. The external auditory canal is red, swollen, and filled with purulent debris; the tympanic membrane appears normal where it can be seen. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas species are the most common cause of acute otitis externa, and swimming is the usual precipitant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Contaminated water enters the outer ear canal and Pseudomonas enters through the small microabrasions created as the skin stretches and swells. Otitis externa presents with pain, redness, and swelling of the outer canal, with purulent discharge in more severe cases, and the pain characteristically worsens with manipulation of the ear. Swimming is the most common cause, and blocking the ears before swimming helps prevent it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter baumannii causes hospital-acquired pneumonia and wound infection, not swimmer's ear in a healthy child.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Haemophilus influenzae likewise causes acute otitis media behind an intact tympanic membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moraxella catarrhalis is one of the classic middle ear pathogens and is not a typical otitis externa organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of middle ear infection (acute otitis media), not the outer ear canal.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has three weeks of worsening left ear pain and drainage despite topical therapy. Granulation tissue is seen in the canal, and he has now developed hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Culture grows an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod. Which of the following best explains his new symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compression of the ear canal by impacted cerumen and debris

choices.label: B
choices.text: Invasion of the skull base involving cranial nerves IX through XII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perforation of the tympanic membrane with a middle ear effusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus within the geniculate ganglion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Septic emboli to the brainstem arising from infective endocarditis

explanation.summary: In diabetics and the immunocompromised, otitis externa can become malignant otitis externa, invading deep tissue and bone and involving cranial nerves IX-XII.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malignant otitis externa presents with symptoms similar to ordinary otitis externa but with far more severe tissue damage. Invasion into deeper tissues, bone, and the bloodstream is possible. Involvement of cranial nerves IX-XII produces difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, and difficulty speaking, and the infection is life-threatening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Impacted cerumen causes conductive hearing loss and fullness; it does not produce cranial nerve palsies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A perforated tympanic membrane causes drainage and hearing loss but leaves the lower cranial nerves intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion causes facial palsy with vesicles, not an oxidase-positive bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infective endocarditis is not suggested here, and emboli would not follow a progressive external ear infection.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman in a burn unit develops septicemia caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The isolate produces exotoxin A, a toxin present in most clinical isolates of this organism. Which of the following best describes how this toxin kills host cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks elongation factor 2, halting host protein synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cleaves ribosomal RNA within the 60S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: It degrades membrane phospholipids and lyses the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters

choices.label: E
choices.text: It raises intracellular cAMP by modifying a G protein

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas exotoxin A blocks elongation factor 2, shutting down protein synthesis and killing the target cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strains of Pseudomonas secrete several toxins that damage host cells, and exotoxin A is present in most clinical isolates. It blocks elongation factor 2 activity, which is critical for translation. Without functioning EF-2 the cell cannot make protein and ultimately dies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inactivation of the 60S ribosomal subunit is the mechanism of Shiga toxin, not exotoxin A.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phospholipase activity that lyses membranes describes the alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens in gas gangrene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking release of GABA and glycine describes tetanospasmin from Clostridium tetani.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising cAMP by modifying a G protein describes toxins such as cholera toxin, heat-labile toxin of ETEC, anthrax toxin, and pertussis toxin.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A wound isolate of Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces a blue pigment that is directly toxic to host cells, including leukocytes and epithelial cells. Which of the following is this pigment?

explanation.summary: Pyocyanin is the blue Pseudomonas pigment that is toxic to leukocytes and epithelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. aeruginosa makes two pigments, pyocyanin and pyoverdine. Pyocyanin is blue and toxic for cells, including leukocytes and epithelial cells, so it contributes directly to tissue damage. Together with pyoverdine it gives colonies their blue-to-aqua appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alginate is the polysaccharide of the mucoid capsule; it is not a pigment and is not cytotoxic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exotoxin A is a secreted protein toxin, not a pigment, and it acts by blocking elongation factor 2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is the gram-negative outer membrane endotoxin and does not color the colony.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyoverdine is the other Pseudomonas pigment, but it is yellow and fluorescent and functions in iron binding.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A flask of Pseudomonas culture glows yellow-green when a ultraviolet lamp is shone on it in a darkened laboratory. The molecule responsible also binds iron for the bacterium. Which of the following is it?

explanation.summary: Pyoverdine is a yellow, fluorescent, iron-binding pigment that makes Pseudomonas fluoresce under UV light.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyoverdine is one of the two pigments produced by P. aeruginosa. It is yellow and fluorescent, and it binds iron. Other Pseudomonas species can produce pyoverdine as well, which is why they fluoresce under ultraviolet light.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alginate forms the mucoid capsule seen in cystic fibrosis isolates and does not fluoresce.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exotoxin A is a secreted protein toxin that blocks elongation factor 2 and has no pigment function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The polysaccharide capsule contributes to adherence and protection, not to fluorescence or iron acquisition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyocyanin is blue and cytotoxic; it is not the fluorescent iron-binding pigment.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: Sputum from an intubated patient grows a motile gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and is oxidase positive. The colonies are blue-green. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: A motile, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod with blue-green colonies is Pseudomonas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas species are gram-negative, do not ferment lactose, and are oxidase positive. They are motile by a single polar flagellum, and pyocyanin and pyoverdine give the colonies an aqua or green color. This combination identifies the organism in the laboratory.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter is a non-motile, oxidase-negative coccobacillus with colorless or creamy colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Escherichia coli also ferments lactose, which separates it from Pseudomonas on MacConkey agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae ferments lactose and does not produce a blue-green pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salmonella does not ferment lactose but is oxidase negative and produces no pigment.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: Two gram-negative rods from different patients both fail to ferment lactose on MacConkey agar; one is later identified as Pseudomonas and the other as a Salmonella species. Which of the following laboratory findings best separates Pseudomonas from non-lactose-fermenting organisms such as Salmonella and Shigella?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ability to grow on standard blood agar

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram stain morphology of the organism

explanation.summary: Oxidase positivity distinguishes Pseudomonas from the other non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two tests anchor the identification of Pseudomonas. The inability to ferment lactose separates it from lactose fermenters such as E. coli and Klebsiella. Oxidase production then separates it from the non-lactose-fermenting gram-negatives such as Salmonella and Shigella, which are oxidase negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All of these organisms grow readily on routine laboratory media.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase is not the test used to distinguish these gram-negative rods from one another.
whyWrongByChoice.C: All are gram-negative rods on Gram stain, so morphology does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: All three organisms in question fail to ferment lactose, so this test cannot tell them apart.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: Sputum from a 17-year-old with cystic fibrosis grows Pseudomonas colonies that are strikingly slimy and wet in appearance, unlike the dry colonies grown from a burn wound isolate on the adjacent plate. Overproduction of which of the following explains this mucoid phenotype?

explanation.summary: The mucoid capsule of Pseudomonas is made of alginate and is characteristic of cystic fibrosis isolates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas can produce a mucoid capsule made of alginate, a polysaccharide that absorbs a large multiple of its own weight in water. Strains expressing this capsule adhere to and colonize mucus far better. Mucoid strains are almost exclusively isolated from the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Exotoxin A is a secreted toxin; in chronically colonized CF lungs these toxins are actually downregulated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is present on all gram-negative bacteria and does not confer the mucoid appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyocyanin is the blue cytotoxic pigment and affects colony color rather than texture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyoverdine is a fluorescent iron-binding pigment and does not create a slimy colony.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: The mucoid capsule that Pseudomonas expresses in the cystic fibrosis lung is a polysaccharide with a striking capacity to hold water, which helps the organism adhere to and colonize airway mucus. Approximately how much water can it absorb relative to its own weight?

explanation.summary: Alginate can absorb roughly 200-300 times its own weight in water.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alginate is the polysaccharide of the Pseudomonas mucoid capsule and absorbs about 200-300 times its weight in water. That water-holding capacity is what makes the colonies visibly slimy and lets the organism bind and colonize the thick mucus of the cystic fibrosis airway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the capacity by roughly two orders of magnitude.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is far below the figure described for alginate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is still well short of the actual water-binding capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This overstates the capacity by about tenfold.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: Pseudomonas isolates recovered from the chronically colonized lungs of cystic fibrosis patients express far fewer secreted toxins than isolates recovered from acute wound infections in other patients. Which of the following best explains this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic exposure selects for strains unable to produce toxins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Host mucus chemically inactivates the secreted bacterial toxins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the polar flagellum prevents export of secreted toxins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxin genes are transferred away to other bacteria in the biofilm

choices.label: E
choices.text: White blood cells penetrate mucus poorly, so toxins are dispensable

explanation.summary: In the cystic fibrosis lung Pseudomonas downregulates most virulence factors because white blood cells cannot reach it through the mucus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas colonizing cystic fibrosis mucus stops producing most of its virulence factors. White blood cells cannot infiltrate the mucus layer well, so the organism can save energy by shutting those factors off. Virulence factor reduction of this kind is uncommon among pathogenic bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics select for resistance, not for loss of toxin production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The toxins are not being made in the first place; this is a change in bacterial gene expression, not chemical inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flagellar loss relates to motility, and toxin secretion does not depend on the flagellum here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gene transfer within a biofilm does not explain the coordinated downregulation seen in these isolates.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with cystic fibrosis has had recurrent pulmonary infections and a steady decline in lung function since childhood. Which of the following is the most common cause of death in patients with this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic cirrhosis from biliary tract obstruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory failure from chronic lung infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Septicemia arising from urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Respiratory failure due to chronic infection is the most common cause of death in cystic fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thick mucus lets bacteria colonize deeper in the lungs and in higher numbers, which drives chronic inflammation. That inflammation progressively destroys the lungs and increases the risk of further infection, a cycle in which Pseudomonas plays a central role. Respiratory failure from these chronic infections is the most common cause of death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liver disease can complicate cystic fibrosis but does not account for most deaths.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intestinal obstruction occurs in cystic fibrosis but is not the leading cause of mortality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic involvement causes malabsorption and is managed with enzyme replacement; it is not the usual cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary tract infection is not a characteristic complication of cystic fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A neutropenic 4-year-old with Pseudomonas bacteremia is noted to have a black, necrotic ulcer with a surrounding rim of erythema in the left axilla. Which of the following is the name of this lesion?

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum is the necrotic skin lesion of disseminated Pseudomonas infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most Pseudomonas diseases are clinically indistinguishable from those of other bacteria, but bacteremia and septicemia can produce a fairly unique presentation: ecthyma gangrenosum. It is a necrotic skin lesion commonly seen alongside hematologic dissemination of the organism, and the anogenital and axillary areas are most commonly involved.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erysipelas is a raised, sharply demarcated superficial streptococcal cellulitis without necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythema migrans is the expanding targetoid rash of early Lyme disease and is not necrotic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hot tub folliculitis produces red follicular papules and pustules, not a black necrotic ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly spreading deep soft tissue infection, not a discrete embolic skin lesion.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with Pseudomonas septicemia is noted to have a new red macule in the groin. If this lesion follows its characteristic course, which of the following sequences is expected over the next 48 hours?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progression to a honey-colored crust, then a healing scar

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progression to a scaling patch, then hypopigmented skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progression to a targetoid plaque, then central clearing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progression to a tender nodule, then spontaneous resolution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progression to pustules and bullae, then a necrotic ulcer

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum begins as a red macule or papule, becomes pustular and bullous, and ends as a necrotic ulcer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ecthyma gangrenosum starts as a red macule or papule. It then develops into pustules and bullae, and finally a necrotic ulcer forms. Recognizing this evolution in a septic patient should raise suspicion for disseminated Pseudomonas, although its absence does not rule the organism out.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Honey-colored crusting describes impetigo, typically caused by staphylococci or streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Scaling followed by hypopigmentation describes a superficial dermatosis rather than an infarcted skin lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A targetoid plaque with central clearing describes erythema migrans, not ecthyma gangrenosum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spontaneous resolution of a tender nodule does not describe this necrotizing lesion.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with third-degree burns over 45% of his body develops a Pseudomonas wound infection on hospital day 8, and the wound bed has a green discoloration. His absolute neutrophil count is markedly low. Which of the following best explains the neutropenia?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of neutrophils by the polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct destruction of neutrophils by secreted exotoxin A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of neutrophils inside the alginate biofilm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of bone marrow function by the burn injury

explanation.summary: The severe tissue damage and inflammation of a third-degree burn can suppress bone marrow and cause neutropenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas typically infects large-area, third-degree burns, colonizing the necrotic tissue and secreting virulence factors that progressively damage host tissue. The severe damage and inflammation caused by third-degree burns can suppress bone marrow function and lead to low neutrophil counts. That neutropenia further increases the risk of severe infection and dissemination, and septicemia is a common complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no autoimmune mechanism operating in this burn patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The capsule aids adherence and protection from phagocytosis, not consumption of neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exotoxin A kills cells by blocking elongation factor 2, but it is not the explanation given for the low neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biofilm formation protects bacteria from immune cells; it does not deplete circulating neutrophils.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman who sleeps in her contact lenses and rarely replaces her lens solution develops a painful red eye with photophobia. Slit lamp examination shows a corneal ulcer with greenish discharge. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: Contact lens misuse is a classic setup for Pseudomonas keratitis, which often causes permanent corneal damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas species can cause severe eye infections, usually after an abrasion or trauma to the eye. Because the organism is common in the environment, it can contaminate and build up in contact lens solution, so poor cleaning or replacement of lenses is a recipe for disaster. Corneal infections caused by Pseudomonas commonly cause permanent damage, and green discharge reflects its pigments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haemophilus influenzae causes conjunctivitis and middle ear disease rather than contact lens keratitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Moraxella catarrhalis is a respiratory tract pathogen and is not implicated here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococcus aureus is a common skin and eyelid pathogen but is not the organism tied to contaminated lens solution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause keratitis but lacks the contact lens solution and green discharge association.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman intubated in the intensive care unit develops fever, purulent tracheal secretions, and a new infiltrate on ventilator day 6. Which of the following is the most common cause of multidrug-resistant ventilator-associated pneumonia?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of multidrug-resistant ventilator-associated pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas is one of the most common causes of pneumonia in hospitals, especially ventilator-acquired pneumonia, and it heads the list of multidrug-resistant pathogens in that setting. Poor host health, intrinsic antibiotic resistance, and the organism's ability to thrive on artificial surfaces such as an endotracheal tube all contribute.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haemophilus influenzae is also grouped with the non-multidrug-resistant pathogens in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MSSA is by definition antibiotic sensitive; MRSA is the resistant staphylococcal counterpart.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serratia marcescens appears among the antibiotic-sensitive Enterobacteriaceae rather than the MDR group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae is listed among the non-multidrug-resistant causes of ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: An intensive care unit isolate from a tracheal aspirate is a non-motile, oxidase-negative gram-negative coccobacillus that forms colorless, creamy colonies and is resistant to carbapenems. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: Acinetobacter is a non-motile, oxidase-negative, non-pigmented gram-negative coccobacillus, in contrast to Pseudomonas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acinetobacter species are gram-negative with a shape between a rod and a sphere, hence coccobacilli. They are non-motile and oxidase negative, and their colonies are colorless or creamy rather than pigmented. They are also extremely resistant to antibiotics, including carbapenems, with some strains resistant to almost everything, so minimum inhibitory concentration testing is needed to guide therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Escherichia coli is a lactose-fermenting bacillus and is not described as a non-motile coccobacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a lactose-fermenting bacillus rather than a coccobacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudomonas is a motile bacillus that is oxidase positive and produces aqua or blue-green pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stenotrophomonas is grouped with Pseudomonas as a closely related organism and is not the coccobacillus described.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: A soldier evacuated from a combat zone with a blast injury to the thigh develops a deep wound infection. Which of the following organisms is characteristically associated with wound infections acquired in war zones and natural disaster areas?

explanation.summary: Acinetobacter baumannii is a classic cause of wound infection in war zones and disaster settings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acinetobacter species are found in water and soil, are very resistant to antibiotics, and target immunocompromised patients. In addition to being a common cause of hospital-acquired infection, they commonly cause wound infections in war zones and natural disaster areas. A. baumannii is the species most often isolated from infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Haemophilus influenzae likewise causes respiratory and middle ear infections, not blast wound infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moraxella catarrhalis is a respiratory pathogen with no association to traumatic wound infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neisseria meningitidis causes meningitis and meningococcemia, not contaminated wound infections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a respiratory tract pathogen causing pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria

questions.stem: An intensive care unit experiences an outbreak of Acinetobacter baumannii affecting six patients over three weeks, and several previously treated patients remain colonized months later. Which of the following best explains how this organism spreads between patients in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosolized water from building cooling tower systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: Airborne droplet nuclei that stay suspended for hours
